content.name: Bone mineral density testing
content.category: Metabolic bone disease and densitometry physics

hook.text: How does dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry subtract soft tissue to measure grams of bone mineral per square centimeter—and why do more than half of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores never cross the -2.5 osteoporosis threshold?

urgency.label: Outpatient preventive and secondary fracture liaison assessment
urgency.context: Central DXA is a non-emergent outpatient test, yet ordering it promptly after any sentinel fragility fracture of the hip, vertebra, humerus, pelvis, or distal forearm—or before initiating long-term systemic glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, or androgen deprivation therapy—prevents recurrent osteoporotic fractures that carry substantial 1-year mortality.

content.review_status: Source checked educational treatise. Independent clinical review pending.

sections.heading: Physics of Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA): Why two photon energies are mandatory

paragraphs.text: A single-energy X-ray beam passing through the human lumbar spine or hip cannot quantify bone mineral content accurately because variations in overlying abdominal fat and lean muscle thickness attenuate the beam unpredictably. Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) solves this two-compartment problem by transmitting two distinct low-dose X-ray photon energies—typically around 40 kiloelectronvolts and 70 to 100 kiloelectronvolts, generated either by rapid K-edge cerium/samarium filtering or fast kilovoltage switching—through the anatomical region of interest. Because high-atomic-number calcium and phosphorus in hydroxyapatite bone mineral exhibit a steep photoelectric attenuation drop between the low- and high-energy beams compared with low-atomic-number soft tissue (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen), solving simultaneous two-energy attenuation equations subtracts out the soft-tissue component pixel by pixel and calculates Bone Mineral Content (BMC, in grams) and projected two-dimensional Bone Area (in square centimeters).

Dividing BMC by projected area yields areal Bone Mineral Density (aBMD, expressed in grams per square centimeter, g/cm2). A fundamental physical limitation follows directly from this formula: DXA measures two-dimensional areal density (g/cm2) rather than true three-dimensional volumetric density (g/cm3). If two individuals have identical true volumetric trabecular and cortical bone density (g/cm3) inside their vertebrae, the taller person with larger, deeper vertebral bodies has a greater thickness of bone along the X-ray path for every square centimeter of projected area and therefore registers a systematically higher areal BMD on DXA, whereas a short, petite adult or growing child with smaller bones registers an artificially lower areal BMD. Radiation dose from a central hip-and-spine DXA scan is extraordinarily low—roughly 1 to 10 microsieverts, equivalent to less than one day of natural background radiation.

sections.heading: T-scores vs Z-scores, the NHANES III reference standard, and WHO diagnostic thresholds

paragraphs.text: Because raw areal BMD values in g/cm2 differ by up to 12 to 15 percent across scanner manufacturers (Hologic, GE Lunar, and Norland use different edge-detection algorithms and dual-energy calibration standards), clinical interpretation converts raw g/cm2 into standardized deviation scores. The T-score compares the patient's measured BMD against the mean BMD of a healthy young-adult reference population at peak bone mass, expressed in standard deviations (SD): T-score equals (Patient BMD minus Young-Adult Mean BMD) divided by 1 Young-Adult SD. To harmonize global diagnosis, the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), World Health Organization (WHO), and Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation mandate a single uniform reference database for femoral neck and total hip T-scores in ALL patients regardless of sex or race/ethnicity: the NHANES III white female aged 20 to 29 years reference database.

In postmenopausal women and men aged 50 years and older, the WHO diagnostic classification applies to the lowest T-score among the lumbar spine (L1–L4), total hip, femoral neck, or 33 percent (one-third) radius: Normal is a T-score of -1.0 or higher; Low Bone Mass (Osteopenia) is a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 (-1.1 to -2.4); Osteoporosis is a T-score of -2.5 or lower; and Severe (Established) Osteoporosis is a T-score of -2.5 or lower in the presence of one or more fragility fractures. In sharp contrast, the Z-score compares the patient's BMD against an age-, sex-, and ethnicity-matched reference population. Per ISCD Official Positions, T-scores must NOT be used in premenopausal women, men under age 50, or children and adolescents; in those younger populations, Z-scores are reported, where a Z-score of -2.0 or lower is defined as 'below the expected range for age' (and a Z-score above -2.0 is 'within the expected range for age'), and osteoporosis cannot be diagnosed on densitometric criteria alone without a clinically significant fracture history.

sections.heading: Anatomical skeletal sites: Lumbar spine L1–L4, proximal femur, and the 33% distal radius

paragraphs.text: A standard central DXA examination measures both the posterior-anterior lumbar spine (L1 through L4) and the proximal femur (evaluating the femoral neck and total hip regions of interest; Ward's triangle and the greater trochanter alone must never be used for diagnostic classification). The lumbar spine is enriched in metabolically active trabecular (cancellous) bone, which has a high surface-to-volume ratio and responds earliest both to estrogen deficiency at menopause and to antiresorptive or osteoanabolic therapy, making the lumbar spine the most sensitive site for serial treatment monitoring when free of degenerative artifact. The total hip and femoral neck contain a higher proportion of cortical bone and represent the single strongest densitometric predictor of hip fracture.

To ensure valid lumbar spine interpretation, all four vertebrae L1–L4 are included unless specific vertebrae are affected by focal structural artifacts. Per ISCD rules, an individual vertebra must be excluded from the spine average if it shows clear focal anatomical abnormality (osteophytes, compression fracture, laminectomy, or pedicle hardware) or if its T-score differs by more than 1.0 standard deviation from the immediately adjacent vertebra; at least two anatomically valid vertebrae are required for a diagnostic lumbar spine report (for example, L1–L3 or L2–L4, never a single vertebra alone). When the spine or both hips cannot be measured or interpreted accurately, or in any patient with primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism (because excess parathyroid hormone catabolizes cortical bone preferentially while preserving trabecular spine bone), the non-dominant forearm 33 percent (one-third) radius—a predominantly cortical site—must be measured.

sections.heading: Positioning and structural artifacts that falsely elevate or depress lumbar and hip BMD

paragraphs.text: Virtually every structural artifact encountered in the aging lumbar spine adds radiodense calcium along the posterior-anterior X-ray beam path and therefore FALSELY ELEVATES measured lumbar spine BMD and T-score, masking true trabecular osteoporosis. The four classic spine culprits are: (1) degenerative spondylosis and facet-joint osteoarthritis with marginal osteophytes and endplate sclerosis; (2) heavily calcified abdominal aortic atherosclerosis lying directly anterior to L1–L4 along the posterior-anterior beam path; (3) osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (where crushed trabeculae compact into a smaller projected area, raising g/cm2 of the fractured body by 0.5 to 1.5 T-score units!); and (4) oral barium contrast, calcium tablets in the bowel, vertebroplasty polymethylmethacrylate cement, or ankylosing spondylitis syndesmophytes. Only posterior surgical laminectomy (bone removal) or lytic bone metastases falsely lower spine BMD.

In the proximal femur, technologist positioning of hip internal rotation is critical. Because the femoral neck angles anteriorly (anteversion) by roughly 15 degrees, the patient's leg must be internally rotated 15 to 25 degrees using a positioning block so the femoral neck axis lies flat and parallel to the scanner table—confirmed visually by seeing minimal or zero lesser trochanter in profile. If the hip is inadequately rotated or externally rotated (seen as a prominent lesser trochanter), the femoral neck is foreshortened along the X-ray projection, which artificially increases measured femoral neck BMD by up to 5 to 10 percent and invalidates serial comparison.

sections.heading: Precision assessment, Least Significant Change (LSC), and serial treatment monitoring

paragraphs.text: When a repeat DXA scan is performed 1 to 2 years after starting bisphosphonate, denosumab, or romosozumab/teriparatide therapy, comparing T-scores across two different scanner brands or comparing a numerical change in g/cm2 without knowing the facility's measurement precision is a major clinical error. T-scores should never be used to calculate serial change because reference database updates or minor rounding shifts alter T-scores independently of bone mass. Instead, serial monitoring must compare absolute areal BMD (in g/cm2) acquired on the exact same DXA machine (or cross-calibrated machines) against the facility's calculated Least Significant Change (LSC) at the 95 percent confidence level.

Per ISCD standards, each DXA facility determines its precision error (root-mean-square standard deviation, in g/cm2) by scanning 30 patients twice or 15 patients three times with full repositioning between scans. Multiplying the precision error by 2.77 yields the 95 percent confidence Least Significant Change (typically ~0.025 to 0.035 g/cm2, or roughly 3 to 5 percent at the lumbar spine and total hip, and wider at the smaller femoral neck). Any change in g/cm2 between baseline and follow-up that is smaller than the LSC lies within random measurement noise and is reported as stable (remembering that stable or rising BMD on antiresorptive therapy represents treatment success, whereas only a statistically significant decline exceeding the LSC signals non-adherence, malabsorption, or secondary bone loss).

sections.heading: Bone density vs Bone quality: Trabecular Bone Score (TBS), Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA), and FRAX

paragraphs.text: Areal BMD captures only 60 to 70 percent of bone's mechanical resistance to fracture; the remaining 30 to 40 percent is governed by bone quality—microarchitectural trabecular connectivity, cortical porosity, bone turnover rate, and collagen cross-linking. Consequently, in large population cohorts such as the National Osteoporosis Risk Assessment (NORA) study of 200,160 postmenopausal women and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF), more than 50 percent of all clinical fragility fractures (including hip and vertebral fractures) occur in women whose baseline BMD falls in the osteopenic (-1.0 to -2.4) or normal range rather than <= -2.5! Why? Because while women with T-scores <= -2.5 have the highest individual relative risk, the osteopenic population is vastly larger in absolute numbers, and many osteopenic patients harbor clinical risk factors or degraded microarchitecture.

Three tools bridge the gap between areal BMD and true fracture risk. First, the WHO Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) integrates femoral neck BMD with 11 clinical risk factors (age, sex, BMI, prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, current smoking, glucocorticoid exposure >= 5 mg/day prednisone equivalent for >= 3 months, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, and alcohol >= 3 units/day) to estimate 10-year absolute probability of hip fracture (pharmacotherapy threshold >= 3 percent in US guidelines) and major osteoporotic fracture (threshold >= 20 percent). Second, Trabecular Bone Score (TBS) analyzes grayscale pixel-to-pixel texture variograms on the existing lumbar spine DXA image to quantify trabecular microarchitecture, independently reclassifying fracture risk in type 2 diabetes (where areal BMD is paradoxically normal or elevated despite fragile cortical pores and advanced glycation end-products) and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. Third, lateral Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA) on the DXA scanner detects clinically silent moderate-to-severe vertebral compression fractures (present in up to 15 to 20 percent of older osteopenic patients), which immediately reclassifies an 'osteopenic' patient as having severe clinical osteoporosis warranting pharmacotherapy.

sections.heading: Population screening guidelines (USPSTF, BHOF, Endocrine Society) and secondary osteoporosis evaluation

paragraphs.text: United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation (BHOF), and Endocrine Society guidelines recommend routine screening central DXA for all women aged 65 years and older, and for postmenopausal women younger than 65 years who have increased clinical fracture risk as determined by a formal clinical risk assessment tool (such as FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk >= 8.4 percent, equivalent to that of a 65-year-old white woman with no other risk factors). BHOF, ISCD, and the Endocrine Society also recommend central DXA testing in men aged 70 years and older, in adults aged 50 to 69 with clinical risk factors or low-trauma fracture, and in any adult initiating long-term glucocorticoid therapy or cancer hormone-deprivation therapy.

Before attributing a T-score <= -2.5 (or a Z-score <= -2.0) to primary postmenopausal or age-related bone loss, clinicians must screen for secondary metabolic causes of bone fragility or osteomalacia. A severe vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia (unmineralized osteoid matrix), which produces a low areal BMD on DXA that is indistinguishable from osteoporosis on the scan alone—yet administering potent intravenous bisphosphonates or denosumab to a patient with unrecognized osteomalacia or hypocalcemia can precipitate life-threatening symptomatic hypocalcemia! Standard baseline laboratory evaluation for newly diagnosed osteoporosis includes serum calcium, albumin, phosphorus, creatinine/eGFR, alkaline phosphatase, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, complete blood count, 24-hour urinary calcium (to detect idiopathic hypercalciuria or occult calcium/vitamin D malabsorption from celiac disease), thyroid-stimulating hormone, and in men morning total testosterone, plus serum/urine protein electrophoresis when vertebral osteopenia/fracture raises suspicion for multiple myeloma.

content.name: Nuclear medicine imaging
content.category: Molecular imaging and radiopharmaceutical physics (PET and SPECT)

hook.text: How do positron annihilation coincidence circuits and gamma cameras map metabolic flux, receptor density, and organ perfusion—and why can recent insulin injection, brown adipose activation, or balanced triple-vessel coronary ischemia make a PET or SPECT scan look deceptively false?

urgency.label: Time-sensitive physiological emergencies (V/Q scan in pregnancy PE, HIDA in acute cholecystitis, GI bleed, testicular torsion) and oncology staging
urgency.context: While oncology PET/CT and receptor theranostics are scheduled outpatient studies, nuclear medicine provides decisive acute diagnostics in suspected acute acalculous or calculous cholecystitis (technetium-99m HIDA cholescintigraphy), pulmonary embolism in pregnancy or contrast-allergic renal failure (ventilation-perfusion SPECT), intermittent lower gastrointestinal bleeding, and suspected cerebrospinal fluid leak.

content.review_status: Source checked educational treatise. Independent clinical review pending.

sections.heading: Radiopharmaceutical physics: Emission from within vs transmission from without

paragraphs.text: Radiography, computed tomography, and DXA are transmission imaging modalities: an external X-ray tube fires photons through the patient toward a detector to map anatomical tissue density. Nuclear medicine reverses this paradigm into emission molecular imaging: a trace chemical quantity (nanograms to micrograms, typically devoid of any pharmacologic mass effect) of a biologically targeted molecule labeled with an unstable radioisotope—a radiopharmaceutical—is administered intravenously, orally, or by inhalation, and external detectors map where the physiological pathway concentrates or excretes the tracer. Consequently, nuclear medicine reveals cellular metabolism, osteoblastic bone turnover, hepatobiliary excretion, glomerular filtration vs tubular secretion, and neuroendocrine or prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) receptor expression long before anatomical organ contour changes on CT or MRI.

Clinical nuclear medicine divides into two primary detector architectures governed by nuclear decay physics: Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET). SPECT tracers—most commonly Technetium-99m (Tc-99m, physical half-life 6.01 hours, emitting a monoenergetic 140-kiloelectronvolt gamma ray), Iodine-123 (159 keV, half-life 13.2 hours), and Indium-111—emit single gamma photons isotropically. Because gamma rays cannot be focused by an optical lens, a gamma camera or SPECT gantry places a heavy lead collimator perforated by thousands of parallel or pinhole channels in front of a sodium iodide thallium-activated scintillation crystal (or solid-state cadmium-zinc-telluride detector) so only photons traveling perpendicular to the crystal reach the detector—rejecting > 99.9 percent of emitted photons and limiting spatial resolution to roughly 7 to 12 millimeters.

sections.heading: Positron annihilation, 511-keV coincidence detection, and hybrid PET/CT attenuation correction

paragraphs.text: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) achieves higher sensitivity and finer spatial resolution (~4 to 5 millimeters) without mechanical lead collimators by exploiting the physics of antimatter-matter annihilation. Proton-rich PET radionuclides—such as Fluorine-18 (F-18, physical half-life 109.8 minutes), Gallium-68 (Ga-68, half-life 67.7 minutes), Copper-64, and Rubidium-82 (half-life 75 seconds)—decay by emitting a positively charged positron (beta-plus particle). After traveling a short positron range in tissue (roughly 0.6 millimeters in water for low-energy F-18 positrons, vs ~2.9 mm for Ga-68 and ~5.9 mm for Rubidium-82), the positron loses kinetic energy and annihilates with an ambient electron, converting their combined rest mass via Einstein's mass-energy equivalence directly into two high-energy 511-kiloelectronvolt gamma photons fired in nearly opposite directions (180 degrees apart).

A ring of fast lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO/LYSO) scintillation detectors surrounding the patient registers a valid positron event only when two detectors on opposite sides of the ring record 511-keV photons within a narrow coincidence timing window of 4 to 12 nanoseconds ('electronic collimation'), localizing the annihilation along the line of response. Modern Time-of-Flight (TOF) PET measures the picosecond arrival-time difference between the two 511-keV photons (300 picoseconds equals a 4.5-centimeter localization segment along the line of response), boosting effective signal-to-noise ratio especially in large patients. In hybrid PET/CT and SPECT/CT scanners, a co-registered low-dose or diagnostic CT scan serves two vital functions: it provides precise anatomical localization for every metabolic hot spot, and it generates a voxel-by-voxel linear attenuation map (mu-map) at 511 keV or 140 keV to correct for photon absorption inside deep thoracic and abdominal structures.

sections.heading: F-18 FDG metabolic trapping, patient preparation traps, and Standardized Uptake Value (SUV) physics

paragraphs.text: The workhorse radiotracer of oncologic, infectious, and neurologic PET/CT is 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18]fluoro-D-glucose (F-18 FDG). Like dietary glucose, F-18 FDG enters cells via facilitated glucose transporters (particularly GLUT1 and GLUT3, which are strongly overexpressed in most malignant tumors due to the Warburg aerobic glycolysis effect, as well as in activated macrophages and neutrophils) and is phosphorylated by hexokinase into F-18 FDG-6-phosphate. Because FDG lacks the 2-hydroxyl group required for isomerization by phosphoglucose isomerase into fructose-6-phosphate, FDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed down the glycolytic pathway and—in tissues with low glucose-6-phosphatase activity—remains metabolically trapped inside the cell proportional to the tissue's glycolytic rate.

Strict pre-analytical patient preparation is mandatory because F-18 FDG competes directly with endogenous blood glucose and responds to circulating insulin. Patients must fast for at least 4 to 6 hours prior to FDG injection with serum blood glucose confirmed below 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), avoid strenuous exercise for 24 hours, and rest quietly in a warm room during the 60-minute uptake phase. If a patient eats a carbohydrate meal or receives rapid-acting insulin shortly before FDG injection, hyperinsulinemia translocates GLUT4 transporters to the cell membranes of all skeletal and cardiac myocytes, shunting the entire FDG dose into diffuse skeletal muscle ('insulin scan' / 'superscan of muscle') and starving tumor lesions of tracer—causing false-negative oncology staging! Conversely, cold ambient room temperature triggers sympathetic beta-3 adrenergic activation of thermogenic brown adipose tissue in the supraclavicular, cervical, axillary, and paravertebral regions, creating intense bilateral symmetric FDG uptake that can mask or mimic nodal lymphoma metastases. Semi-quantitative Standardized Uptake Value (SUVmax or SUVmean)—defined as tissue radioactivity concentration (kBq/mL) divided by injected dose (MBq) normalized to body weight (kg) or lean body mass (SUL)—depends on exact uptake time (60 vs 90 minutes), blood glucose level, partial-volume averaging in lesions smaller than 8 to 10 mm, and respiratory motion at the lung bases/liver dome.

sections.heading: FDG-non-avid malignancies and receptor-targeted PET (Ga-68/Cu-64 DOTATATE and F-18/Ga-68 PSMA)

paragraphs.text: A critical clinical error is assuming that a negative F-18 FDG PET/CT rules out cancer across all histologies. Several well-differentiated malignancies exhibit low GLUT1 expression, low hexokinase activity, or high glucose-6-phosphatase dephosphorylation and are notoriously FDG-non-avid (false-negative on FDG PET): well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors (low Ki-67 grade 1 and 2 carcinoid and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors), prostate adenocarcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinomas (mucinous colorectal, gastric signet-ring, and ovarian carcinomas where sparse tumor cells float in acellular mucin pools), well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma (which retains high glucose-6-phosphatase that dephosphorylates FDG-6-P and exports it back out of the cell), renal cell carcinoma (also obscured by normal urinary excretion of FDG in the renal collecting system), low-grade bronchoalveolar/lepidic lung adenocarcinoma, and low-grade marginal zone or small lymphocytic lymphomas.

Modern receptor-targeted molecular PET overcomes these FDG blind spots and pairs diagnostic imaging directly with targeted radioligand therapy ('theranostics'). Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors overexpress cell-surface somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) and are imaged with high sensitivity (> 92 percent) using Gallium-68 or Copper-64 DOTATATE PET/CT, selecting patients for Lutetium-177 DOTATATE peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Similarly, prostate carcinoma cells strongly overexpress transmembrane Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA); Ga-68 PSMA-11 or F-18 DCFPyL (piflufolastat F-18) PET/CT detects sub-centimeter nodal and osseous metastases at very low serum PSA levels (0.2 to 1.0 ng/mL) during biochemical recurrence—where conventional CT and technetium bone scans are almost invariably negative—and selects metastatic castration-resistant patients for Lutetium-177 PSMA-617 therapy.

sections.heading: Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (SPECT and PET): Relative flow reserve and the 'balanced ischemia' trap

paragraphs.text: Nuclear myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) evaluates the hemodynamic significance of epicardial coronary artery disease and microvascular dysfunction by comparing regional left ventricular radiotracer uptake at peak stress (exercise or vasodilator stress with regadenoson, adenosine, or dipyridamole—noting that methylxanthines/caffeine within 12 to 24 hours block A2A adenosine receptors and cause false-negative vasodilator stress tests!) against resting uptake. SPECT MPI uses Technetium-99m sestamibi or tetrofosmin (lipophilic cations sequestered inside cardiomyocyte mitochondria proportional to regional blood flow), whereas cardiac PET MPI uses Rubidium-82 or Nitrogen-13 ammonia. Normal myocardium shows homogeneous tracer uptake at both stress and rest; a reversible perfusion defect (reduced uptake at stress that normalizes at rest) indicates inducible myocardial ischemia; and a fixed defect (absent uptake at both stress and rest, confirmed by F-18 FDG viability PET if hibernating myocardium is suspected) indicates myocardial infarction scar.

Every clinician interpreting a normal SPECT myocardial perfusion scan must understand the physical limitation of relative perfusion normalization—the 'balanced triple-vessel or left main ischemia' trap. Conventional SPECT scales the brightest pixel in the left ventricular myocardium to 100 percent of the color bar and displays all other wall segments relative to that peak segment. If a patient has severe flow-limiting stenosis in all three major coronary arteries (LAD, LCx, and RCA) or severe left main disease that reduces peak hyperemic blood flow uniformly across the entire left ventricle by 50 percent, the brightest segment is itself ischemic, yet all walls scale evenly to 100 percent and the relative SPECT perfusion map can look deceptively 'normal'! Indirect warning clues of balanced ischemia on SPECT include transient ischemic dilation (TID) of the left ventricular cavity on post-stress vs rest images, stress-induced drop in gated LVEF, increased lung-to-heart uptake ratio, and ischemic ECG changes during vasodilator infusion. Quantitative cardiac PET MPI solves this trap directly by measuring dynamic first-pass tracer kinetics to calculate absolute Myocardial Blood Flow in mL/min/g of tissue and Coronary Flow Reserve (the ratio of peak stress flow to rest flow, normally > 2.0).

sections.heading: Targeted organ scintigraphy: Bone scans (flare phenomenon), HIDA, V/Q, and Renal MAG3 vs DTPA

paragraphs.text: Technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate (Tc-99m MDP) planar and SPECT skeletal scintigraphy ('bone scan') does not image tumor cells directly; instead, bisphosphonate tracers chemisorb onto hydroxyapatite crystals in proportion to local osteoblastic bone remodeling and regional blood flow. Consequently, osteoblastic metastases (prostate and breast cancer) light up intensely, whereas purely osteolytic lesions with minimal reactive osteoblast activity—classic in multiple myeloma, renal cell carcinoma, and thyroid cancer—are frequently cold or invisible on bone scan (making whole-body low-dose CT, MRI, or FDG PET the preferred skeletal tests in multiple myeloma!). Furthermore, when a patient with metastatic breast or prostate cancer responds successfully to systemic chemotherapy or hormone therapy, healing osteoblastic repair inside previously occult or lytic metastases causes a temporary surge in Tc-99m MDP uptake and apparent 'new' bone-scan lesions during the first 3 to 6 months of treatment—the 'osteoblastic flare phenomenon,' which must not be mistaken for disease progression when clinical pain and tumor markers are improving.

Three targeted physiologic studies provide definitive organ functional diagnosis. First, Tc-99m hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA / mebrofenin) cholescintigraphy evaluates suspected acute cholecystitis: hepatocytes extract the tracer from blood and excrete it into the biliary tree within 15 to 30 minutes; visualization of the gallbladder within 60 minutes (or after intravenous morphine augmentation, which contracts the sphincter of Oddi to raise common bile duct pressure and drive bile into a patent cystic duct) rules out acute calculous cholecystitis with > 95 percent negative predictive value, whereas persistent non-visualization of the gallbladder at 4 hours (or 30 minutes post-morphine) with normal common bile duct-to-duodenum transit confirms cystic duct obstruction (recognizing that prolonged fasting > 24 hours, total parenteral nutrition, or severe hepatocellular failure can cause false-positive non-visualization). Second, pulmonary Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy (pairing inhaled Tc-99m DTPA/Technegas or Xenon-133 ventilation with intravenous Tc-99m macroaggregated albumin particles 10 to 90 micrometers in size that lodge transiently in < 0.1 percent of pulmonary precapillary arterioles) diagnoses acute pulmonary embolism when two or more large segmental perfusion defects occur in regions of normal ventilation ('V/Q mismatch,' PIOPED II High Probability) and is the diagnostic test of choice for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Third, dynamic renal scintigraphy uses Tc-99m MAG3 (cleared ~90 percent by proximal tubular secretion, preferred in obstructed or immature kidneys) or Tc-99m DTPA (cleared by glomerular filtration) with furosemide diuresis: a dilated renal pelvis caused by non-obstructive hydronephrosis washes out rapidly after furosemide (half-time T1/2 < 10 minutes), whereas true mechanical ureteropelvic junction or ureteral obstruction retains tracer with a prolonged washout T1/2 > 20 minutes.

sections.heading: Radiation safety, pregnancy and lactation protocols, and hybrid attenuation artifacts

paragraphs.text: Effective radiation doses in nuclear medicine vary by radiopharmaceutical and hybrid CT protocol: a pulmonary perfusion scan delivers ~1 to 2 millisieverts (with markedly lower maternal breast radiation dose than CT pulmonary angiography, an important consideration in pregnant patients with normal chest radiographs), a bone scan ~4 to 6 mSv, an F-18 FDG PET scan ~5 to 7 mSv from the positron tracer itself (total ~12 to 20 mSv when combined with diagnostic CT), and historical Thallium-201 cardiac scans ~15 to 22 mSv (now largely replaced by lower-dose Tc-99m or Rb-82 protocols). In women of childbearing potential, pregnancy status is verified before diagnostic or therapeutic radionuclide administration; notably, therapeutic Iodine-131 (beta-plus-gamma emitter used for hyperthyroidism and differentiated thyroid cancer ablation) crosses the placenta and permanently destroys the fetal thyroid gland if given after 10 to 12 weeks of gestation, making pregnancy an absolute contraindication to I-131! For lactating mothers, most Tc-99m and F-18 diagnostic studies require either no interruption or a brief 4- to 24-hour pumping interruption depending on free pertechnetate fraction (per NRC and ICRP guidelines), whereas I-131 requires complete cessation of breastfeeding for that child.

Finally, hybrid PET/CT and SPECT/CT interpretation requires inspecting both the CT-attenuation-corrected (AC) and uncorrected (NAC) emission images. If a patient breathes or shifts between the rapid 5-second CT acquisition and the 15-minute PET emission scan, the liver dome on CT is misregistered over the right lung base on PET, causing the scanner to under-correct attenuation and create an artificial 'cold' defect at the diaphragmatic dome. Conversely, dense metallic hip prostheses, spinal hardware, or concentrated intravenous/oral barium contrast on CT cause the attenuation-correction algorithm to over-correct local 511-keV photon loss, creating an artificial 'hot' hypermetabolic artifact on the AC PET image that disappears completely when checked on the non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET dataset.

sections.heading: Documented clinical cohorts: proPSMA randomized trial, PIOPED II V/Q study, and Lugano PET lymphoma response

paragraphs.text: Landmark prospective trials with exact denominators establish the diagnostic superiority of modern molecular imaging over conventional anatomical staging. In the multicenter Australian proPSMA randomized controlled trial of 302 men with biopsy-proven high-risk localized prostate cancer randomized to first-line Gallium-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT versus conventional abdominal/pelvic CT plus technetium-99m bone scan (Hofman et al., The Lancet 2020), PSMA PET/CT achieved a 27-percentage-point greater diagnostic accuracy for pelvic nodal or distant metastatic disease than conventional imaging (92 percent vs 65 percent; p < 0.0001), altered clinical management intent in 28 percent of men versus 15 percent with conventional imaging, yielded fewer equivocal findings (7 percent vs 23 percent), and delivered less than half the total patient radiation dose (8.4 mSv vs 19.2 mSv; p < 0.001).

In suspected acute pulmonary embolism, the prospective PIOPED II investigation (Sostman et al., Radiology 2008) evaluated 733 patients with V/Q scintigraphy against composite reference standards: when interpreted using modified PIOPED II criteria excluding indeterminate studies, a high-probability V/Q scan had a sensitivity of 77.4 percent for PE and a very low-probability or normal V/Q scan had a specificity of 97.7 percent (with negative predictive value > 96 percent when paired with low or intermediate clinical probability). In Hodgkin and FDG-avid non-Hodgkin lymphomas, the Lugano Classification (Cheson et al., Journal of Clinical Oncology 2014) replaced anatomical CT size criteria with the 5-point Deauville PET scale comparing residual lesion FDG uptake against internal physiological reference organs: Scores 1 (no uptake) and 2 (uptake <= mediastinal blood pool) and Score 3 (uptake > mediastinal blood pool but <= normal liver parenchyma) define a Complete Metabolic Response even when a fibrotic residual mediastinal mass persists on CT, whereas Scores 4 and 5 (uptake moderately or markedly above liver or new lesions) identify residual active lymphoma requiring treatment escalation.

content.name: Blood pressure measurement

hook.text: A blood pressure reading helps answer whether pressure is too high or too low. The cuff, setting and repeated record determine how confidently that question can be answered.

sections.heading: What the two numbers describe

paragraphs.text: Blood pressure is the pressure of blood against the walls of arteries, the vessels carrying blood away from the heart. The top number, systolic pressure, describes the peak as the heart pumps; the bottom number, diastolic pressure, describes the lower pressure between beats. Results are reported in millimetres of mercury, abbreviated mmHg: 130/80 means two pressures, not a fraction to divide. High blood pressure often causes no symptoms, so feeling well cannot establish a normal result. Measurement may investigate dizziness or fainting, screen for otherwise silent hypertension, or monitor treatment. The clinical question changes the meaning of the same number: a routine check, a symptom assessment and monitoring during serious illness are different tasks. This chapter concerns adult human measurement; children and pregnancy require their own interpretation pathways.

sections.heading: How a cuff produces a result

paragraphs.text: A cuff temporarily compresses an artery in the upper arm. With the auscultatory method, a trained observer uses a stethoscope to hear Korotkoff sounds as cuff pressure falls. Their appearance and disappearance identify systolic and diastolic pressure. Most electronic monitors instead sense small pressure pulses in the cuff and use a calculation to estimate the two values; this is called the oscillometric method. The machine is not listening with a hidden stethoscope. Its particular calculation and cuff matter, so different models are not automatically interchangeable. Automated office systems can take several measurements after a rest period and average them, with staff present or absent. Manual measurement also needs training and equipment checks. Neither method becomes dependable merely because the display has precise digits. A catheter inside an artery measures pressure directly in selected hospital situations; ordinary cuff measurements are indirect estimates.

sections.heading: Preparing a reproducible seated measurement

paragraphs.text: For routine home measurements, the American Heart Association advises avoiding smoking, caffeine and exercise during the preceding 30 minutes, emptying the bladder, and resting quietly for at least five minutes. Use a bare upper arm, avoid talking or using the phone, and support the arm so the middle of the cuff is at heart level. Sit with the back supported, feet resting flat and legs uncrossed. Follow the monitor's fitting instructions rather than placing its cuff over clothing. At each session, take two readings one minute apart and record both. Agree on measurement times and frequency with the clinician. A record should preserve the actual numbers rather than only the lowest one. Bringing the monitor to an appointment lets staff check technique, fit and agreement with office equipment. A home result should inform the agreed treatment plan; it is not a reason to stop prescribed medication independently.

sections.heading: Cuff size has a measured effect

paragraphs.text: Cuff labels describe the arm circumference range for a particular cuff and monitor. A cuff that closes around an arm is not necessarily the correct size. In the 2023 Cuff(SZ) randomized crossover trial, 195 adults had repeated automated measurements using appropriate and inappropriate cuff sizes. When a regular cuff was used on participants who needed an extra-large cuff, systolic pressure averaged 19.5 mmHg higher than with the appropriate cuff; when a large cuff was required, the average excess was 4.8 mmHg. These were group comparisons under the study protocol, not a correction table for an individual. Subtracting 19.5 from somebody's result would introduce an unsupported estimate. The useful response is to measure the arm, obtain the compatible cuff and repeat the measurement correctly. Repeating an incorrectly fitted cuff many times can reproduce the same systematic error.

sections.heading: Arm position can move the numbers

paragraphs.text: The 2024 ARMS randomized crossover trial studied 133 adults using an automated monitor. Compared with a supported arm on a desk with the cuff at heart level, resting the hand on the lap increased systolic pressure by an average 3.9 mmHg; leaving the arm unsupported at the side increased it by 6.5 mmHg. Diastolic pressure also rose. This experiment measured differences in readings, not later strokes or medication injuries. The side position changed both height and support, so the result does not isolate one mechanism. It nevertheless makes a practical point: an arm dangling from an examination table is a different measurement condition. A repeat performed in the same poor position may look reassuringly consistent while retaining the same bias. The study averages should not be used to adjust a person's recorded pressure arithmetically.

sections.heading: Home monitoring needs a complete schedule

paragraphs.text: NICE's UK adult pathway, updated in February 2026, uses two seated home readings at least one minute apart, morning and evening, for at least four days and ideally seven. It discards day one and averages the remaining readings. Its diagnostic framework pairs clinic pressure at least 140/90 with daytime ambulatory or home average at least 135/85 mmHg; either component can be raised. These are specified UK criteria, not universal treatment targets. Hypothetical arithmetic example, not a patient: four retained readings of 140/88, 136/86, 132/82 and 128/80 have mean systolic pressure 134 and mean diastolic pressure 84 mmHg. Average each column separately. Four readings alone do not satisfy that complete monitoring schedule. An average made from selectively saved readings is also not the average required by the protocol. Ask which schedule and threshold the local service is using.

sections.heading: Ambulatory monitoring follows a day and night

paragraphs.text: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, or ABPM, uses a wearable recorder and cuff to collect repeated measurements during usual waking activity and sleep, commonly over 24 hours. It answers a different question from a few quiet home readings. The report should distinguish waking, sleeping and whole-record averages, identify how many readings were usable, and show individual measurements with their times. A diary of actual sleep, symptoms, activities and medication timing helps explain the record; clock time alone may misclassify a night worker's sleep. Cuff inflation can disturb sleep or be uncomfortable, and movement can interfere with individual measurements. Missing or erroneous readings need review before a smooth-looking average is accepted. A night-time pattern is an interpretation of a recording obtained under particular conditions, not a diagnosis from one isolated peak. Follow the fitting service's instructions and report a disturbed or atypical night.

sections.heading: Validation is evidence about a device

paragraphs.text: A validation study compares a monitor with a reference method using a defined protocol, a range of pressures and arms, and rules for judging disagreement. The AAMI/ESH/ISO collaboration explains why testing needs adequate participants, cuff representation and separate consideration of special populations. Validation is about the tested model and configuration; a familiar brand name is not enough. Evidence in ordinary adults does not automatically establish performance in pregnancy, very young children, unusually large arms or atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. Importantly, passing a protocol does not guarantee that every individual's reading is accurate. The collaboration explicitly acknowledges remaining individual errors. Ask whether the exact monitor, compatible cuff and intended population have appropriate validation evidence. A repeated discrepancy with clinical measurements warrants checking the patient, technique and equipment rather than assuming either the home device or the clinic must always be right.

sections.heading: Wearable claims need a specific check

paragraphs.text: The US Food and Drug Administration warned in September 2025 about unauthorized products claiming to measure or estimate blood pressure, including software on smartwatches and rings. A number appearing in a health app does not establish that the feature has been evaluated for this medical purpose. The agency recommends checking the exact device name and intended use in its authorization records and discussing an appropriate authorized device when care depends on the result. This warning does not mean every wearable is unauthorized, or that all products have identical capabilities. Product status can change. Authorization for one feature also should not be assumed to cover a separate blood pressure claim. A seller's medical-looking advertisement, a wellness score and an authorized blood pressure measurement function are different pieces of information. Do not use an unverified estimate as the sole reason for changing medication or delaying assessment of concerning symptoms.

sections.heading: Standing pressure asks another question

paragraphs.text: Orthostatic hypotension means a sustained pressure fall after standing: conventionally at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes. It can coexist with high resting pressure. The 2024 AHA scientific statement describes assessment after a period lying down, followed by standing measurements; the timing, starting posture and symptoms affect what is detected. A single normal seated result cannot exclude a posture-related problem. Clinicians consider patterns, medicines, other illness and the person's risk of falls rather than treating every low reading as the same condition. Do not attempt unsupported standing measurements when fainting or unsteadiness makes standing unsafe. Recording when dizziness occurs and whether it follows standing gives the clinical team a useful question to investigate. The aim is to understand pressure regulation and symptoms together, rather than simply pursuing the lowest possible seated number.

sections.heading: Actual case: low arm pressure concealed higher pressure elsewhere

paragraphs.text: Nasrullah and colleagues reported a 59-year-old woman with severe vascular disease, anemia and dark stools whose pressure was initially 64/55 mmHg. Fluids, transfusions and escalating vasopressors, medicines that raise pressure, did not normalize arm readings. Even catheters in both wrist arteries recorded low pressures. On day four, a femoral artery catheter measured 174/71 while a wrist catheter measured 64/50 mmHg. Review of imaging identified severe narrowing of the arteries supplying both arms. Treatment was redirected using lower-limb measurements, and vasopressors were stopped within 24 hours. The outcome was not an uncomplicated recovery: the report describes strokes, ventilator-associated pneumonia and delirium during a prolonged admission; a later successful vascular repair is not documented. This was a site-dependent pressure problem, not proof that the cuff's electronics had failed. One case neither establishes its frequency nor justifies dismissing ordinary low pressures as artifact.

sections.heading: Actual case: hypertension was a clue to an obstructed aorta

paragraphs.text: Jurcut and colleagues described an adult woman with hypertension difficult to control despite several medicines. Arm pressures were 145/80 and 135/80 mmHg, but examination found no palpable femoral or more distal leg pulses. Echocardiography and CT identified coarctation, a narrowing of the aorta, the main artery leaving the heart. A catheter measured a 70 mmHg pressure difference across that narrowing. After balloon treatment and placement of a covered stent, the catheter gradient fell below 10 mmHg and leg pulses returned. She was discharged three days later. At six months, pulses remained present, low-dose antihypertensive treatment was still needed, and ultrasound showed a residual peak gradient of 27 mmHg. Ultrasound and catheter gradients are different measurements. The case illustrates why pressure, pulses and anatomy are interpreted together; it does not show that a routine arm result alone can identify the cause of hypertension.

sections.heading: Office and home disagreement can be informative

paragraphs.text: The 2025 AHA/ACC adult guideline recommends averaging repeated measurements rather than treating a single office value as usual pressure; at least two readings on at least two occasions can reduce error. It uses US hypertension categories beginning at systolic 130 or diastolic 80 mmHg, illustrating why the guideline and setting must accompany a label. White-coat hypertension describes high office but lower out-of-office pressure in an untreated person; masked hypertension describes the reverse. These are documented patterns, not proof that a patient is anxious or a monitor faulty. Hypothetical example, not a published patient: clinic 150/92 and a properly collected home average 128/78 suggest a possible white-coat pattern, requiring confirmation and follow-up. The reverse discrepancy also warrants attention. In treated people, related terms are white-coat effect and masked uncontrolled hypertension. Both records remain relevant; selecting whichever number is preferred defeats the purpose of measuring in two settings.

sections.heading: An outcome trial explains why targets require context

paragraphs.text: The SPRINT final report analyzed 9,361 participants at increased cardiovascular risk who did not have diabetes or previous stroke, randomized to systolic targets below 120 or below 140 mmHg. During the intervention period, with median follow-up 3.33 years, the primary combined cardiovascular outcome occurred at 1.77% per year with intensive treatment versus 2.40% per year with standard treatment. The hazard ratio was 0.73, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.63–0.86. That comparison concerns the rate over follow-up, not a 27 percentage point reduction in a person's absolute risk. The combined outcome included heart attack, other acute coronary syndromes, stroke, acute heart failure and cardiovascular death. Several serious adverse events, including hypotension, electrolyte abnormalities, acute kidney injury and syncope, were more frequent with intensive treatment. This supports an assessed treatment strategy in the trial population; it does not make its target a universal home-reading instruction or prove that measurement alone prevented events.

sections.heading: Home readings can improve care when somebody acts on them

paragraphs.text: In TASMINH4, 1,182 adults with treated but inadequately controlled hypertension were randomized in UK general practices to usual clinic-guided care, self-monitoring, or self-monitoring with electronic transmission of results. General practitioners used the readings to adjust treatment. At 12 months, 1,003 participants contributed to the primary available-case analysis. Compared with usual care, adjusted clinic systolic pressure was lower by 3.5 mmHg in the self-monitoring group and 4.7 mmHg in the transmission group. The difference between those two intervention groups was not statistically established. Adverse events were similar across groups. These are actual trial results for blood pressure control, not demonstrated reductions in deaths or strokes during this study. The intervention connected a measurement schedule to clinical review and medication decisions. Merely purchasing a monitor or collecting an ever-longer spreadsheet does not reproduce that care process; agree who reviews results, how they are shared and when feedback should occur.

sections.heading: When a reading needs prompt action

paragraphs.text: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline defines severe hypertension in nonpregnant adults using systolic pressure above 180 or diastolic above 120 mmHg. Either component can cross its threshold; both do not have to be raised.

The AHA's public guidance distinguishes very high pressure without new concerning symptoms from a possible emergency. Without emergency symptoms, repeat a very high reading after at least one minute. If it remains very high, contact a health professional as soon as possible. If pressure is in that range with chest pain, breathlessness, new weakness or numbness, visual change or difficulty speaking, call the local emergency service immediately; do not wait for pressure to settle. Pregnancy has a separate pathway. Keep the reading, time and medicine list available. Routine confirmation and emergency assessment serve different purposes.

Do not let a reassuring home estimate delay assessment of severe new symptoms, or improvise medication changes from an unverified device result. An unauthorized wearable can miss an important pressure change as well as generate a false alert.

content.name: Pulse oximetry
content.hook: How can a bright oxygen percentage be useful at the bedside and still conceal a dangerous problem with breathing or oxygen delivery?

sections.heading: What the display is estimating

paragraphs.text: A pulse oximeter uses light to estimate arterial hemoglobin oxygen saturation, usually displayed as SpO2. It also reports a pulse rate; these are separate measurements, and neither alone diagnoses the cause of breathlessness. At home, the FDA advises following the particular device's instructions, keeping the hand warm and relaxed, avoiding movement, removing nail polish from the measurement finger, and waiting for a steady reading. Recording the time, reading, and symptoms makes a trend more interpretable than an isolated screenshot. Poor circulation, temperature, pigmentation, and other conditions can affect accuracy even when a number appears. Device category matters too: some over-the-counter medical-purpose oximeters have FDA clearance, whereas general-wellness or sporting products are not evaluated for clinical decisions. Buying without a prescription does not, by itself, identify which category applies. The measurement should be read alongside how the person looks and feels and the monitoring plan agreed with their clinical team.

sections.heading: How two colors become an oxygen percentage

paragraphs.text: Oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently. A conventional oximeter illuminates tissue and detects how the received light changes through the pulse cycle. The pulsating component helps distinguish changing arterial blood volume from background absorption. Photoplethysmography, the optical recording of these volume-related changes, provides the signal from which the device compares the two colors. The ratio is converted through calibration into the displayed saturation estimate. The FDA's 2024 technical summary describes typical red and infrared wavelengths near 660 and 940 nanometers; exact optical designs vary. A transmission sensor detects light passing through tissue, whereas a reflectance arrangement detects returning light. Neither directly counts oxygen molecules or continuously samples arterial blood. Movement, an inadequate arterial signal, or additional light-absorbing substances can violate the assumptions behind the conversion. Understanding this pathway explains why a plausible display may still need confirmation when it conflicts with the clinical situation.

sections.heading: A cleared device has a particular scope

paragraphs.text: The FDA record for the MD300W512, MD300W314, and MD300W314B4 wrist oximeters illustrates why the model and intended use belong in the interpretation. Its 2018 clearance covers measuring, displaying, storing, and transmitting functional arterial saturation and pulse rate in adults, adolescents, children, and infants, with spot checking or data collection in specified settings. It is a prescription device. This is not a blanket statement about all wrist wearables, every sensor attachment, or every clinical purpose. A clearance applies to the described system and indications, rather than to the general idea of shining light at skin. A downloaded series of readings therefore still requires the device identity, suitable sensor, population, and recording conditions to be meaningful. A device capable of storing data has not automatically been established as a diagnostic test for the cause of nocturnal desaturation, sleep apnea, or a particular respiratory disease. Those questions may require a wider clinical investigation.

sections.heading: Worked example oxygenation is not ventilation

paragraphs.text: Consider an invented patient who becomes drowsy after a respiratory-depressant medicine while receiving supplemental oxygen. The pulse oximeter reads 98%. This is a hypothetical interpretation exercise, not a published case or a recommendation to adjust treatment. The number cannot establish that ventilation, movement of air sufficient to remove carbon dioxide, is adequate. SpO2 estimates hemoglobin saturation; PaO2 is the partial pressure of oxygen dissolved in arterial blood, and PaCO2 is its carbon dioxide counterpart. They answer different questions. The British Thoracic Society guideline advises blood-gas assessment when respiratory-depressant exposure or otherwise unexplained confusion raises concern for carbon dioxide retention. Supplemental oxygen can preserve an apparently satisfactory saturation while ventilation remains impaired. The unresolved question is therefore not simply whether the oxygen percentage is high enough, but whether breathing and acid-base balance are adequate. Clinical examination and appropriate blood gases or respiratory monitoring can answer questions the optical percentage cannot.

sections.heading: Published validation consumer numbers and arterial measurements

paragraphs.text: Harskamp and colleagues compared ten popular consumer oximeters with simultaneous arterial measurements in 35 intensive-care patients, DOI 10.1136/bmjresp-2021-000939. They obtained 2,258 oximeter readings alongside 234 arterial samples. None of the tested consumer devices met the study's cited overall accuracy criterion, although negative predictive values for its defined hypoxemia outcome were high in that particular sample. Predictive value depends on how often the condition occurs in the tested population; it cannot be carried unchanged into every home setting. The investigation excluded hemodynamically unstable patients and evaluated specific products available then. It did not test every inexpensive device sold in 2026 or establish a universal rule that all consumer measurements are unusable. It demonstrates why apparent agreement at many ordinary readings does not ensure that an individual low value, or a reassuring value in an ill person, is correct. Validation should address clinically consequential errors, not merely whether two sets of readings rise and fall together.

sections.heading: Published cohorts a disparity hidden by an ordinary display

paragraphs.text: Sjoding and colleagues' 2020 report, DOI 10.1056/NEJMc2029240, compared pulse oximetry with arterial co-oximetry in hospital data. In its Michigan subset with displayed SpO2 of 92% to 96%, arterial saturation below 88% occurred in 88 of 749 measurements from Black patients, compared with 99 of 2,778 from White patients. These are measurement pairs within a defined display band, not population-wide percentages of people with undiagnosed hypoxemia. The investigators found a similar disparity in a separate multicenter cohort. Race was a recorded patient category, not a direct measurement of skin melanin, and cannot specify the exact error for a particular person. The study highlights clinically important overestimation that can hide low arterial saturation. It does not support subtracting a fixed number from everyone in one racial group. Discordance deserves assessment using the actual patient, signal, device, and, when indicated, a direct arterial comparison rather than an identity-based correction formula.

sections.heading: Pigmentation evidence from a controlled experiment

paragraphs.text: A laboratory experiment answers a somewhat different question from a hospital-record study. Bickler, Feiner, and Severinghaus tested three named oximeter systems in eleven darkly pigmented and ten lightly pigmented healthy volunteers, DOI 10.1097/00000542-200504000-00004. During controlled oxygen-saturation plateaus, the systems overestimated arterial saturation more in the darkly pigmented group, especially at low saturation. The experiment directly examined pigmentation groups under controlled conditions, helping separate this issue from the use of race as a proxy in routine records. Its small volunteer sample and the particular 2005 devices limit generalization to every contemporary sensor or clinical situation. Healthy volunteer accuracy also cannot fully reproduce shock, motion, tissue changes, or the rapidly changing physiology of illness. The experiment establishes that optical measurement can interact with pigmentation; it does not tell a home user how many points to add or subtract. Better validation needs representative participants and clinically relevant conditions, not confidence based on a single average error.

sections.heading: Published outcome cohort beyond measurement disagreement

paragraphs.text: Fawzy and colleagues studied 24,504 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 at 186 US facilities, DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.30856. Pulse oximetry more often overestimated arterial saturation in recorded minority racial and ethnic groups. In a subset of 8,635 patients without an immediately recognized treatment indication, an unrecognized oxygen-based indication was associated with slower receipt of remdesivir or dexamethasone and higher odds of 30-day hospital readmission. The study did not find an association with in-hospital mortality or length of stay. This is outcome evidence beyond simply demonstrating a difference between instruments, but it remains observational. It cannot establish that an individual measurement error caused a particular readmission or that correcting an oximeter alone would prevent it. Recorded race and ethnicity were not direct skin-pigmentation measurements. The treatment context was a particular pandemic-era pathway, so its decision criteria should not be reused as universal oxygen or emergency thresholds for unrelated patients.

sections.heading: What current regulatory proposals do and do not establish

paragraphs.text: The FDA's January 2025 pulse-oximeter guidance proposes updated performance testing and labeling recommendations for medical-purpose devices, including better assessment across skin pigmentation. On the date checked, 7 November 2026, the official page still identifies it as draft guidance, not for implementation. That status matters: a proposal is not a final rule and does not retroactively validate every product already in use. Conversely, the existence of a draft is not evidence that all prior measurements are invalid. The clinical issue remains whether a particular system performs adequately for its intended population and decision. A clear description should distinguish a manufacturer's claimed performance, the conditions used to demonstrate it, and independent clinical evidence. Useful questions include whether darker pigmentation was represented, which saturation range was tested, and how poorly performing or absent signals were handled. An average accuracy statistic can conceal a subgroup difference or a clinically important individual error.

sections.heading: Published case normal pulse oximetry during carbon monoxide poisoning

paragraphs.text: Roth and colleagues reported a 53-year-old woman with vomiting, diarrhea, unilateral headache, tingling, and palpitations, DOI 10.1016/j.jemermed.2009.05.017. The report appeared online in 2009 and in the 2011 journal issue. Conventional pulse oximetry was described as normal, while a cutaneous carbon monoxide oximeter indicated carboxyhemoglobin, COHb, of 28%. The accessible primary abstract does not give the ordinary SpO2 number or a separate laboratory blood COHb result. She received oxygen with noninvasive positive-pressure support. Investigators found a malfunctioning water heater in her residence; the reported COHb fell to normal, she felt well, and she was discharged the next day. This is an actual example of misleading reassurance from conventional oximetry, but one successful detection does not establish the accuracy of every noninvasive CO monitor. The case facts are limited to the primary abstract; unreported neurological follow-up or blood confirmation should not be supplied from inference.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide needs a different analytical question

paragraphs.text: Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide. Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish this situation from normally oxygenated blood. CDC guidance recommends clinical assessment and COHb testing, commonly using multiwavelength laboratory co-oximetry on venous or arterial blood. This technique separates additional absorbing hemoglobin species rather than applying the ordinary two-color assumption. The time since exposure ended and oxygen already received can substantially change the measured COHb. A concentration therefore needs that history and does not closely track every patient's severity or later outcome. Suspected carbon monoxide exposure with significant symptoms, breathing difficulty, confusion, or collapse warrants emergency assessment now; a reassuring finger reading does not make waiting safe. Follow-up also matters because neurological effects may emerge after apparent initial improvement. The questions are whether exposure occurred, which hemoglobin forms are present, and how the patient is affected, rather than whether the ordinary SpO2 has crossed a single cutoff.

sections.heading: Published case benzocaine changed the hemoglobin being measured

paragraphs.text: Nappe and colleagues described a 29-year-old man with weakness, breathlessness, headache, dizziness, and grayish skin after self-treatment of toothache with benzocaine gel, DOI 10.1155/2015/670979. His SpO2 was 88% despite supplemental oxygen. Arterial testing showed PaO2 178 mmHg and a reported calculated saturation of 99%, but co-oximetry measured oxyhemoglobin 71.9% and methemoglobin 27.4%. These are different quantities, not competing measurements that can simply be averaged. After intravenous methylene blue, his symptoms improved; repeat co-oximetry showed methemoglobin 0.9%. He was discharged after four hours with symptoms resolved and advice to stop the exposure and obtain dental care. The full primary case supports this immediate outcome, not a long-term prognosis or a safe amount of benzocaine. It illustrates why a high dissolved oxygen pressure or calculated saturation can coexist with abnormal hemoglobin chemistry and impaired effective oxygen carriage. Co-oximetry resolved the discrepancy that an ordinary pulse percentage could not.

sections.heading: Methemoglobin changes the optical assumptions

paragraphs.text: Methemoglobin contains oxidized ferric iron rather than the usual ferrous iron and cannot carry oxygen normally. Inherited disorders or acquired oxidant exposures can increase this fraction. The EHA and EuroBloodNet consensus, DOI 10.1002/ajh.26340, emphasizes unexpected pulse-oximeter results or discordance with clinical appearance as reasons to investigate. With appreciable methemoglobin, many conventional instruments tend toward a reading near 85%, with limited ability to track the true severity. That characteristic behavior is not a diagnostic cutoff or a way to estimate the methemoglobin percentage from the screen. A plateauing SpO2 can conceal either deterioration or improvement. Laboratory measurement of the hemoglobin fractions and consideration of medications, chemicals, and inherited causes are needed. Severe symptoms require emergency assessment, whereas a stable person with a mild incidental finding needs a different evaluation pathway. The purpose of additional testing is to identify the abnormal absorber and its clinical effects, not simply to find another instrument displaying a preferred oxygen number.

sections.heading: Published trial detection and patient outcomes are different endpoints

paragraphs.text: Moller and colleagues randomized 20,802 surgical patients to perioperative pulse-oximetry monitoring or no such monitoring in a 1993 trial, DOI 10.1097/00000542-199303000-00007. Detected hypoxemia increased markedly with monitoring, and clinicians changed care more often. This does not mean the monitor caused the oxygen abnormalities; it made otherwise unrecognized episodes visible. The study did not find a significant reduction in overall postoperative complications, in-hospital deaths, or hospital stay. Its primary abstract supports those trial-level findings, not detailed reconstruction of individual participants or contemporary monitoring systems. The distinction remains useful: detection, response to detection, and improved clinical outcomes are separate links in a pathway. A tool may reveal a problem without a particular trial demonstrating a downstream mortality benefit. Equally, failure to show such a benefit in this setting does not establish that oximetry is useless in another population or that it can safely replace examination, staffing, or other respiratory monitoring.

sections.heading: Worked example a percentage is not the amount carried

paragraphs.text: Consider two explicitly hypothetical people with the same SpO2 of 97% but very different hemoglobin concentrations. Their percentage of available hemoglobin carrying oxygen may be similar while their total oxygen-carrying capacity differs substantially. This is an explanatory comparison, not a reported patient pair, transfusion rule, or treatment threshold. An oximeter does not measure how much hemoglobin is present. Jay and colleagues studied seventeen nonhypoxemic patients with acute severe anemia, DOI 10.1016/S0196-0644(94)70158-X, and found small average differences between pulse and arterial saturation. That finding is compatible with the teaching example: an accurate saturation percentage can coexist with anemia and does not quantify oxygen delivery to tissues. Their small study did not establish accuracy under every combination of severe anemia, low saturation, or circulatory failure. When oxygen delivery is the clinical question, a blood count, circulatory assessment, and the underlying cause may matter alongside saturation rather than being replaced by it.

sections.heading: Published forensic case beyond any living finger measurement

paragraphs.text: Tabian and colleagues reported an 80-year-old man with impaired mobility who died in an outdoor fire involving vegetation and household waste, DOI 10.1111/1556-4029.14649. The article appeared online in 2020 and in the 2021 journal issue. Postmortem femoral blood contained COHb 73.7% and hydrogen cyanide 1.3 micrograms/mL. Cyanide was analyzed 48 hours after death, limiting reconstruction of its concentration at death. Autopsy and toxicology documented severe burns and substantial toxic exposures; the authors discussed contributions from carbon monoxide and cyanide rather than providing a living oxygen-monitoring record. No premortem SpO2 was reported, so this cannot be presented as an observed pulse-oximeter failure or a case in which a particular monitor would have prevented death. No premortem treatment sequence is reported. The forensic contribution is the need for complementary analytes and anatomical findings when reconstructing a fatal fire. A pulse percentage, a blood hemoglobin fraction, a toxicant concentration, and tissue injury answer related but distinct questions and should retain their specimen and clinical context.
