content.name: Canine tick borne pathogen testing

hook.text: An antibody screen for tick-borne pathogens can be positive in a healthy dog and negative early in a sick one. What connects the result to illness?

sections.heading: Start with the dog, then identify the test target

paragraphs.text: This chapter concerns dogs; canine test interpretations and treatment evidence should not be transferred directly to cats. A tick panel usually combines several separate questions. Serology detects antibodies, the immune system's response to exposure. Polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, detects selected pathogen DNA, or genetic material, in the submitted specimen. A blood count measures effects on the animal, including anemia (too few red cells) and reduced platelets, which help blood clot. These observations are related but not interchangeable. The Companion Animal Parasite Council (CAPC) recommends combining history, examination, serology, PCR and hematology for ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis. A dog with unexplained bleeding or marked illness needs prompt assessment while the cause is investigated. A screening result alone cannot establish the severity, date or source of an infection, and antibodies can persist after clinical recovery.

sections.heading: Geography and travel decide which organisms belong on the list

paragraphs.text: The European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites (ESCCAP) guidance distinguishes infections by pathogen, vector and distribution. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma are bacteria; Babesia are single-celled parasites; Borrelia are spiral-shaped bacteria. They are not one interchangeable tick fever. Different tick species carry different agents, and the important species of Babesia vary between regions. A clinician therefore needs the dog's lifetime travel, importation, previous homes, tick prevention and transfusion history, not just its current address. Imported infection can appear where local transmission is uncommon. Conversely, seeing a tick species in an area does not prove that every tick carries a particular pathogen. European, North American and Australian recommendations answer different local questions. A panel suitable for one region may leave out an important organism in another.

sections.heading: Ehrlichia and Anaplasma occupy different blood cells

paragraphs.text: Ehrlichia canis primarily involves monocytes, a type of white blood cell. Anaplasma phagocytophilum involves neutrophils, another white cell, whereas Anaplasma platys infects platelets and can produce cyclic changes in platelet counts. The European practitioner guideline explains why a stained blood smear may reveal bacterial clusters called morulae, yet a negative smear is weak evidence against infection: clusters can be scarce or transient. Antibodies also take time to appear, and related species can cross-react on serology. A genus-level positive may therefore need species-specific PCR to clarify the organism. Paired quantitative antibody measurements, collected during illness and later convalescence, can show a rising response; a single positive titer, or antibody level, may reflect older exposure. PCR before antibiotics can provide complementary evidence. The laboratory needs the actual specimen and treatment history because suppressed or intermittent circulation can produce a negative blood PCR in an infected dog.

sections.heading: A controlled study shows why the first antibody test can miss illness

paragraphs.text: Moroff and colleagues studied eight dogs experimentally infected with Ehrlichia canis and compared PCR with three antibody methods. On the day a reduced platelet count was first detected, PCR was positive in all eight dogs; the antibody methods detected seven, four and one, respectively. After antibiotic treatment began, the blood PCR became negative while antibodies remained detectable. This experiment connects disagreement to the changing biological target, rather than assuming that one result must be a clerical mistake. It also demonstrates product-specific performance: assays designed around different antigens need not become positive together. The small experimental study and its 2014 test versions cannot supply a permanent ranking of every present-day brand. The useful clinical question is which method fits the suspected stage of infection.

sections.heading: A real anaplasmosis case had negative antibodies and a positive PCR

paragraphs.text: A published Vancouver Island case illustrates the early diagnostic gap. The dog's clinical history and a blood smear showing morulae in a neutrophil suggested anaplasmosis. A combination screening test was negative, including its Anaplasma antibody component. After consultation with the laboratory, PCR on the submitted serum detected Anaplasma DNA. The dog improved substantially after a few days of veterinary therapy and had an uneventful recovery. It shows why a negative exposure screen should not end investigation when the examination and cell findings point elsewhere. It does not establish serum as the preferred specimen for every laboratory: the submitted material must match the laboratory's validated assay and the veterinarian's diagnostic question.

sections.heading: Another dog appeared to have lymphoma until the findings were integrated

paragraphs.text: In a 2025 report, a four-year-old Golden Retriever developed fever, poor appetite and lameness after numerous ticks had been removed. Screening antibodies were negative. Joint fluid contained unusual T lymphocytes, a type of immune cell. Flow cytometry, which classifies cells by their features, plus a clonality test supported concern for lymphoma. Blood PCR instead identified Anaplasma phagocytophilum. The dog improved with doxycycline alone, so cancer treatment was deferred. At the follow-up examination 28 days after hospitalization, the clinical signs and platelet abnormality had resolved; repeat joint testing no longer showed the aberrant cell population. Clonality means that many cells share an origin; in this unusual patient it did not establish cancer independently of context. The report supports a comprehensive investigation, not a claim that every clonal result or swollen joint is infection.

sections.heading: Modern assay comparisons still measure a specific reference standard

paragraphs.text: A 2026 comparison evaluated two commercial antibody systems against indirect fluorescent antibody testing. Anaplasma analysis included 310 retained canine serum samples and Ehrlichia analysis 309. Detection did not differ significantly for Anaplasma, whereas the laboratory multiplex system was more sensitive for Ehrlichia relative to that reference. Sensitivity describes detection among reference-positive samples; specificity describes exclusion among reference-negative samples. Neither quantity is the chance that a particular positive dog is sick. The investigators also examined a separate regional sample set and found positivity rates that differed from CAPC reporting. Selection of submitted samples, antigen design and the reference test all matter. These data help choose an exposure screen; they do not turn an antibody result into proof of active clinical disease.

sections.heading: A panel can miss a disease because it never included it

paragraphs.text: Wong and colleagues compared a historical rapid screening assay with molecular testing in 100 pet dogs and 100 stray dogs in Hong Kong without obvious clinical signs. The methods disagreed for some Ehrlichia and Anaplasma results, and the rapid test did not include Babesia, the most frequently detected arthropod-borne infection in that cohort. Another important finding came from sequencing: several initially Ehrlichia-positive PCR products were actually Wolbachia DNA, from bacteria associated with heartworm. This demonstrates why target specificity and confirmatory identification matter even for molecular tests. A negative panel only addresses its listed targets; a positive amplification signal depends on assay design and quality control. These selected dogs and older products do not describe the prevalence or accuracy of all current panels.

sections.heading: Lyme antibodies usually establish exposure before they establish an explanation

paragraphs.text: The American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) Lyme consensus emphasizes that most Borrelia-seropositive dogs remain clinically well. Compatible fever and painful swollen joints can support suspected Lyme arthritis, but other causes and coinfections still need consideration. The consensus also recommends assessment for protein loss in urine in seropositive dogs. Proteinuria means protein is escaping into urine; it requires interpretation with urine sediment, kidney measurements and other possible causes. The serious syndrome called Lyme nephritis remains a presumed association rather than something established by one antibody result. The panel describes important gaps in proving that kidney immune complexes are Borrelia-specific in a living dog. Human Lyme symptoms and testing rules should not be copied directly into canine care; feline clinical disease is even less well established.

sections.heading: For Lyme testing, the antigen named on the report matters

paragraphs.text: A Lyme antibody test is named partly for the bacterial material it uses to capture the dog's antibodies. CAPC describes C6-based testing as a way to distinguish natural exposure from responses detected by some whole-cell assays after vaccination. Vaccination therefore belongs on the request form, together with the product when known; it should not be used to dismiss every positive result automatically. Borrelia burgdorferi also differs from the blood-cell organisms discussed earlier. It resides mainly in tissues, so whole-blood PCR is generally a poor way to exclude canine Lyme infection, and a routine blood smear will not reveal it. A negative broad blood PCR and positive Lyme antibodies can consequently be biologically compatible rather than contradictory. Clinical interpretation must stay linked to the organism and specimen.

sections.heading: Antibody timing can help without providing an exact infection date

paragraphs.text: Wagner and colleagues followed dogs after experimental Borrelia infection and compared several antibody targets. Antibodies against OspC and C6 appeared as early as three weeks, while OspF responses appeared later in that experiment. OspC responses subsequently peaked and declined, whereas other responses increased across the observation period. The researchers also examined sera from 125 client-owned dogs. These findings explain why a laboratory may report different antibody patterns rather than a single Lyme label. They do not create a calendar precise enough to identify the particular walk, tick or household responsible. Experimental challenge, repeat environmental exposure and vaccine composition can alter interpretation. A quantitative antibody value is an immune measurement, not a direct bacterial count, severity score or independent prediction of kidney failure.

sections.heading: Related Borrelia can sometimes cross-react with Lyme assays

paragraphs.text: A controlled study infected seven Beagles with Borrelia turicatae, a relapsing-fever organism distinct from the usual Lyme agent. Six developed a measurable antibody response to that organism. Five of those six reacted on at least one of the evaluated Lyme-associated assays, especially a whole-cell fluorescent antibody method. The two C6 assays remained negative at their diagnostic thresholds. None of the dogs developed the monitored clinical signs during daily observation. This is a bounded finding about particular assays and an experimental exposure, not evidence that every Lyme result is unreliable. It shows why an unexpected pattern in a dog with unusual travel or exposure deserves a laboratory discussion. Cross-reaction means recognition of related material; it does not establish two simultaneous infections.

sections.heading: Babesia testing asks about a red-cell parasite and its species

paragraphs.text: Babesia multiply within red blood cells. Destruction of infected cells, together with immune removal of cells, can produce anemia; some dogs also develop low platelets and other complications. A stained blood smear can show the parasites, but low parasite numbers can make a carrier's smear negative. Whole-blood PCR can identify parasite DNA and help distinguish species that look similar microscopically. Antibodies may cross-react and may still be absent early. CAPC distinguishes larger and smaller canine Babesia because their behavior and treatment response differ. A generic positive result therefore warrants attention to the identified species and method. Improvement after therapy does not automatically demonstrate eradication, and relapse can occur when a persistent infection is unmasked by illness or immune suppression.

sections.heading: A Canadian Babesia case improved, but follow-up did not prove clearance

paragraphs.text: A twelve-year-old American Staffordshire Terrier on Prince Edward Island was referred for suspected immune-mediated destruction of red cells. Blood-film findings suggested Babesia, and PCR with sequencing identified Babesia vulpes. Transfusion support improved the dog's condition, and species-directed treatment followed. Five days after completing that course, the owner reported that the dog was doing well; anemia had improved but remained mild, and no parasites were seen on the reviewed smear. Financial constraints prevented a follow-up PCR. The reported outcome was clinical improvement with a defined laboratory trend, not molecular proof of permanent clearance. The case also illustrates why apparently unfamiliar local diagnoses deserve consideration when the blood findings fit. A historical impression that a region is low risk cannot exclude an individual infection.

sections.heading: A fatal coinfection case shows why urgency follows the patient's condition

paragraphs.text: An Indian case report described a two-month-old puppy with a week of vomiting and poor appetite, pale mucous membranes, severe anemia and low platelets. A blood smear showed organisms consistent with Babesia and Ehrlichia, and molecular testing confirmed the reported coinfection with Babesia canis vogeli and Ehrlichia canis. Despite treatment, the puppy died that same day. This single report does not provide a mortality percentage for all coinfected dogs, and it cannot separate precisely how much each infection contributed. Its practical lesson is that laboratory identification can arrive in a patient already requiring urgent supportive care. Marked weakness, pallor, bleeding or systemic deterioration should not be reduced to an argument about which screening spot is positive before the animal is assessed.

sections.heading: Healthy positive dogs and regional surveys answer a different question

paragraphs.text: A 2025 Townsville study sampled 301 domestic dogs at least six months old through a convenience sample involving clinics and university contacts. None tested positive for Ehrlichia canis, while nine, or three percent, were PCR positive for Babesia vogeli. The population consisted of healthy dogs, so these findings directly illustrate infection detection without a corresponding clinical illness at sampling. They cannot show that Ehrlichia was absent from all dogs in the region, particularly sick or unsampled animals. Nor does a three-percent estimate transfer to puppies, shelters or another country. A regional prevalence figure describes who was sampled, when and how. Those details influence the meaning of a screening result just as much as the printed name of the assay.

sections.heading: Blood donation requires a separate screening decision

paragraphs.text: ACVIM's North American donor-screening consensus treats healthy blood donors differently from dogs being evaluated for illness. A donor can carry a blood-borne agent without obvious signs, and transfusion places material directly into a susceptible recipient. For selected organisms, combining antibody and PCR testing helps address their different detection windows; neither method alone excludes every carrier. The consensus considers regional exposure and specific agents rather than assuming that a general wellness panel makes blood safe. It does not recommend routine Borrelia screening of healthy canine donors in the same way as agents with established blood-borne concerns. Donor eligibility is consequently a veterinary blood-bank assessment. An owner should disclose travel, previous positive tests and treatment history even when the prospective donor currently appears healthy.

sections.heading: Forensic investigation cohorts show risk without diagnosing an animal's history

paragraphs.text: In a multi-state dogfighting investigation, researchers tested 269 seized dogs. Babesia gibsoni was detected in 39 percent using the study's combined testing definition, and infection was associated with anemia. The study distinguished antibody-positive and PCR-positive counts and considered blood exposure through bites and transmission from dam to offspring as possible routes. These are findings in a documented investigation cohort; a positive dog elsewhere has not thereby been proved to have fought. Breed, scars or a pathogen result alone cannot identify a perpetrator or reconstruct a transmission event. In an individual welfare investigation, retain identification, collection dates, laboratory methods, body-condition findings, injuries and the broader scene evidence. The study supports medical screening and anemia monitoring during rescue, rather than replacing the investigation with a test result.

sections.heading: Clinical recovery, negative blood PCR and eradication are distinct outcomes

paragraphs.text: In an experimental Ehrlichia canis study, ten dogs were treated during different phases of infection. Dogs treated in acute or subclinical phases became blood-PCR negative as clinical measurements improved; chronically infected dogs remained intermittently positive. Ticks subsequently fed on treated dogs could still become PCR positive. This research outcome explains why one negative blood sample cannot prove that every relevant tissue is free of organisms. It also differs from demonstrating that each PCR-positive tick would transmit disease to another dog; the measured result was DNA detection in the acquisition-fed ticks. Follow-up must therefore combine the clinical course, blood-cell recovery, specimen timing and an appropriate laboratory plan. Repeated antibiotics simply to make an old antibody result disappear are not an interpretation strategy.

sections.heading: Australian guidance adds a specific long-term and biosecurity context

paragraphs.text: Australia first detected locally acquired canine ehrlichiosis in 2020. Its national veterinary guidance describes the challenge of managing apparently recovered and subclinical dogs in affected regions: antibodies can persist, and a negative blood PCR does not assure that tissue-associated infection has cleared. The guidance advises considering previously diagnosed dogs potentially subclinically infected for life and maintaining appropriate owner education and vector protection. That is a region-specific management stance, not a prediction that every positive dog will develop fatal chronic disease. Illness can emerge long after travel, so previous residence remains relevant. Local veterinarians also handle the applicable reporting requirements and movement advice. Preserve the full timeline when a dog is rehomed; replacing the record with a single recovered label can conceal information needed for future care.

sections.heading: There is no single safe tick attachment clock for every pathogen

paragraphs.text: Fourie and colleagues studied Anaplasma transmission using infected ticks on dogs and an artificial feeding system. All three dogs whose ticks remained until engorgement developed detectable DNA and antibodies; none of the groups with removal at the earlier tested times did, and all dogs remained healthy. Yet pathogen DNA appeared much earlier in some artificial feeding chambers. These findings distinguish transfer of detectable material, establishment of infection and development of clinical illness. They should not be converted into an owner rule that every tick removed before a particular hour is harmless. Tick species, pathogen, inoculum and experimental conditions matter, and other canine agents can transmit faster. The appropriate response is prompt tick management and suitable prevention, with testing planned around the dog's actual exposure and clinical condition.

sections.heading: A useful follow-up plan includes prevention and a durable record

paragraphs.text: CAPC recommends year-round tick control because exposure varies geographically and seasonally, and brown dog ticks can maintain infestations in homes or kennels. Finding a tick despite preventive treatment does not by itself prove that the product was never used; environmental pressure and reinfestation also matter. The veterinary team should match prevention to species, region and the household rather than borrowing another animal's product. Dogs can also signal shared environmental tick exposure for people, who need their own medical assessment if ill. Keep the pathogen name, antibody or DNA target, specimen, collection date, treatment dates and follow-up findings together. That record helps the next clinician distinguish a new illness from an old exposure signal and decide which unresolved question actually needs another test.

sections.heading: Choose and preserve samples for the question being asked

paragraphs.text: The American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) 2026 One Health guidance explicitly separates exposure tests from tests directed at current tick-borne infections. Its diagnostic table lists antibodies, blood smears and PCR as complementary approaches with different limits. It also stresses proper collection and preservation, communication about financial constraints and clinical interpretation of discordant results. For an owner, the practical preparation is a concise timeline and a complete list of drugs, previous results and travel. The veterinary team selects blood or tissue specimens and the laboratory handles validated methods and controls. When several infections are possible, a positive first result need not explain every abnormality. Decide what a further test could change: immediate care, organism identification, donor eligibility, follow-up or regional disease reporting. That purpose makes repeat testing interpretable.

content.name: Leptospira testing in dogs
content.hook: Why can a dog with a serious infection have a negative early test, and what changes when the test detects antibodies rather than bacterial DNA?

sections.heading: The disease and the diagnostic question

paragraphs.text: Leptospirosis is an infection caused by bacteria in the genus Leptospira. In dogs, it can range from an unnoticed infection to serious kidney injury, liver dysfunction, lung disease or death. A serovar is a strain grouping distinguished by features recognized by antibodies; many can infect dogs, and the locally important types vary. The testing question is therefore more specific than whether a dog has ever encountered the organism. Clinicians ask whether current illness is attributable to leptospirosis, whether the organism or its DNA is present, and what precautions are needed. These questions require different evidence. Dogs of any breed or lifestyle can be affected, including small urban pets.

sections.heading: MAT measures the immune response

paragraphs.text: The microscopic agglutination test, abbreviated MAT, detects antibodies in serum, the liquid portion of clotted blood. The laboratory mixes serial dilutions of serum with live leptospiral antigens and looks for clumping. A titer describes the greatest dilution still meeting the test's reaction endpoint. Thus a titer of 1:800 is a dilution result, not a count of 800 bacteria. Laboratories test panels of serovars, and a panel may not represent every possible infecting strain. Cornell also warns that damaged or fatty specimens can hinder interpretation. The test is not a direct measurement of protective immunity after vaccination. A negative reaction cannot settle every suspected case, particularly if the relevant organism is poorly represented by the panel.

sections.heading: A time sequence is stronger than one isolated titer

paragraphs.text: The updated ACVIM consensus recommends combining evidence rather than diagnosing from a single positive or excluding infection from a single negative MAT. Early in disease, a dog may not yet have produced a detectable antibody response. Paired acute and convalescent samples can show seroconversion, meaning a change from undetectable to detectable antibodies, or a substantial rise in titer. The consensus describes repeating serum after roughly one to two weeks when appropriate. The ordering veterinarian coordinates timing with the testing laboratory. PCR, which detects DNA, can provide evidence before antibodies appear. Vaccination dates, onset of illness and antibiotic exposure all affect interpretation. Whenever feasible, diagnostic specimens are collected before treatment, but an ill dog should not wait for convalescent antibodies before receiving necessary care. A plan for repeat testing is part of managing uncertainty, rather than an instruction to leave a worsening patient untreated.

Miller and colleagues showed that the same serum need not yield identical MAT results at every laboratory. They submitted samples from 18 research colony dogs, nine vaccinated, and 17 dogs with clinical leptospirosis to as many as five diagnostic laboratories. Results differed between laboratories and over time, and the identity of the most reactive serogroup was not consistently reproducible. The study therefore cautioned against using the largest titer as a reliable identification of the infecting strain. This matters when someone tries to infer whether a vaccine failed or which animal supplied the infection. A high response to a named antigen is an antibody observation. Determining the actual infecting organism can require culture and molecular characterization. Keeping paired samples within a coordinated laboratory process also makes comparisons more interpretable.

sections.heading: Vaccination can change antibody results

paragraphs.text: A 2025 field study followed 97 healthy dogs after revaccination against four leptospiral serovars. Antibodies to vaccine serovars were detected in all dogs during follow up, and 71 still had detectable antibodies at 52 weeks. Reactions to nonvaccine serovars also occurred. The investigators could not completely exclude natural exposure, but the timing of many increases supported a vaccine response. This observation prevents a common mistake: assuming that an antibody reaction to a serovar outside the vaccine necessarily proves infection with that serovar. It also shows why the date and product name of a recent vaccine are useful diagnostic information. Its outcomes should not be turned into a clinical disease rate.

A companion publication examined five commercial antibody tests using the same 97 dog cohort, so it is not an independent second population. Test responses after revaccination differed substantially. At two weeks, 18 dogs were positive on WITNESS Lepto, compared with 43 on SNAP Lepto and 81 on ImmunoComb in that study. These tests recognize different antibody signals, including immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G, often abbreviated IgM and IgG. Results therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable simply because the devices all carry the word Lepto. This was an investigation of vaccination effects in healthy dogs, not a full comparison of diagnostic accuracy in critically ill patients. A clinic result needs the exact test name, vaccination history and supporting investigations.

sections.heading: PCR looks for DNA in a particular specimen

paragraphs.text: Polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, amplifies selected DNA sequences until they can be detected. Unlike MAT, it does not wait for the dog to make antibodies. However, it can only detect target material present in the submitted sample. Blood and urine can yield different results as infection evolves. Washington State's diagnostic laboratory accepts particular specimen types, specifies storage and transport, and warns that antibiotic treatment can reduce detection. Insufficient sample volume can also lead to a limitation being recorded on the report. These are laboratory requirements, not instructions for owners to collect invasive samples. The practical owner contribution is an accurate timeline: when signs began, when each specimen was collected, and which medicines had already been given. A negative urine PCR is an observation about that specimen and assay, rather than proof that every organ was free of infection.

Martin, Heseltine and Creevy evaluated a PCR assay against a MAT based clinical classification in 43 dogs, using 49 submitted specimens. Seventeen dogs were classified as having leptospirosis and 26 as not having it. Urine PCR sensitivity was approximately 69 percent, while blood PCR sensitivity was 25 percent in the much smaller blood sample group. Specificity was 100 percent in this dataset. Sensitivity describes detection among classified cases; specificity describes exclusion among classified noncases. The reference classification itself had limitations, and the result does not establish perfect specificity everywhere. Nor does it mean blood PCR is intrinsically unhelpful: illness timing and the small numbers mattered. The study supports using complementary testing when suspicion remains, rather than assuming one negative assay always closes the investigation.

sections.heading: A persistent DNA signal needs its own question

paragraphs.text: Hetrick and colleagues followed 32 dogs initially diagnosed through urine PCR. Twenty achieved a negative urine PCR within 14 days or less with the expected antimicrobial approaches, while 12 remained positive after a course of doxycycline lasting as long as 18 days. The published study investigated subsequent testing and treatment, not a simple universal clearance deadline. PCR is a DNA observation, whereas growing an organism in culture is a different demonstration. Persistent positivity therefore needs interpretation alongside illness, treatment history and the laboratory method; it is not an owner instruction to lengthen or switch antibiotics. Likewise, clinical improvement and disappearance of a molecular signal are different outcomes. Follow up may need to establish both the dog's organ recovery and the meaning of continued detection, while retaining appropriate handling precautions.

An asymptomatic carrier is an animal harboring an organism without recognized illness. Carmona Gasca and colleagues described viable Leptospira isolates from asymptomatic dogs as well as fatal cases in Mexico. Four isolates came from kidneys or urine among 58 dogs in a selected canine control setting, with additional isolates from other investigated dogs. Culture supplied evidence beyond an antibody reaction alone. It demonstrates that appearance alone cannot determine whether an animal might shed organisms. It also explains why a positive urine result and the cause of current illness are related questions rather than identical ones. The veterinarian must decide how the test fits the dog's clinical condition and exposure setting.

sections.heading: A fatal suspected case remained unconfirmed

paragraphs.text: Howard reported a six year old female American bulldog with vomiting, jaundice, severe kidney injury and progressively reduced urine production. Leptospirosis was the leading clinical suspicion. One rapid test was interpreted as faintly positive, but blood and urine PCR and a separate antibody ELISA were negative. Despite hospital treatment, the dog worsened and the owner elected euthanasia on the third hospital day. Kidney and liver PCR and immunohistochemistry, staining designed to identify the organism in tissue, were also negative after death. A MAT was not performed. The report retained leptospirosis as a possibility while discussing alternative causes, including toxic injury. This must remain a suspected case, rather than a confirmed example of a test missing proven leptospirosis. Its evidential lesson is valuable precisely because the final cause was unresolved: a persuasive pattern, treatment failure and a fatal outcome do not manufacture a missing microbiological confirmation.

sections.heading: A confirmed case improved but developed a new complication

paragraphs.text: Cho and colleagues reported a nine year old female mixed breed dog with severe kidney injury, absent urine production and lung involvement. Both blood and urine PCR confirmed Leptospira infection. Continuous renal replacement therapy, which supports blood cleaning when kidneys cannot, helped bridge the period before urine production recovered. On day 13, while blood kidney markers were improving, the dog developed tremors, excessive salivation and altered awareness associated with severe magnesium depletion. Veterinary magnesium treatment rapidly resolved the neurological signs. The dog was discharged on day 20 with improved appetite, activity and urine output. Follow up still showed abnormal renal magnesium handling despite improvement in creatinine. This reported outcome contains both recovery and an important complication. It explains why a confirmed infectious diagnosis or a better creatinine result does not eliminate the need to investigate new signs during recovery.

sections.heading: A postmortem result can clarify a negative living sample

paragraphs.text: Grippi and colleagues investigated a two month old puppy born in a Sicilian municipal kennel. It developed loss of appetite, fever and then jaundice. Urine PCR was negative, while antibody testing showed reactions to leptospiral antigens. The puppy deteriorated and died on the third day. PCR on kidney tissue after death detected pathogenic Leptospira DNA, supporting the diagnosis that the urine sample had not established. Examination also identified intestinal intussusception, where bowel folds into another segment. Testing of the other 66 kennel dogs found antibody positive animals, but no further clinical leptospirosis was observed during monitoring. The kennel introduced movement restrictions, disinfection and rodent control. This is a relevant forensic lesson about combining the clinical record, postmortem tissue findings and microbiology. A tissue PCR result does not by itself establish the exact exposure, prove neglect, or demonstrate that every other finding was caused by the same infection.

sections.heading: Survival figures need the population and the time point

paragraphs.text: In a retrospective referral study, Da Fonseca Ioannou and colleagues described 22 dogs with leptospirosis severe enough to require renal replacement therapy. Sixteen survived to hospital discharge, approximately 73 percent of the original group. Three of those discharged dogs died within 30 days, and 12 were alive at least six months after discharge. Thus survival to discharge and longer survival had different denominators and different meanings. Some surviving dogs continued to have chronic kidney abnormalities. The maximum creatinine concentration did not distinguish survivors from nonsurvivors in this small cohort; broader organ involvement and bilirubin were more informative associations. These observations should not become an individual survival calculator or proof of a treatment effect. They describe selected dogs that reached a center able to provide intensive support, with no untreated comparison group.

A Sydney case series illustrates how different a reported outcome can look in another setting. Seventeen dogs with confirmed leptospirosis were identified between 2017 and 2020. Six died, nine were euthanized and two survived, an overall case fatality of about 88 percent. The two survivors recovered their biochemical abnormalities over subsequent follow up. Several dogs died before a strong antibody response developed; three dogs tested by MAT were negative to all tested serovars. Dialysis was not available locally in that series. The high fatality therefore belongs to that particular outbreak, severity pattern and treatment setting. It cannot be directly compared with the referral dialysis cohort as though the difference measured the benefit of dialysis alone. Case selection, available treatment and euthanasia decisions all influence the number, while negative early serology can complicate recognition.

sections.heading: An outbreak investigation links human and animal evidence

paragraphs.text: A CDC investigation in Wyoming described 13 reported canine cases during a 2023 outbreak. Three met confirmed criteria and ten probable criteria; four dogs died or were euthanized. A human patient with occupational dog exposure also met a probable case definition. The report connected the events epidemiologically, meaning through histories, timing and exposure patterns, rather than presenting a genetically proven transmission chain from a named dog. This distinction matters in occupational health and forensic reasoning. A shared setting may support an exposure hypothesis without identifying the precise source. The investigation also found increased recommendations for canine vaccination after public health outreach. It provides a real example of veterinary recognition contributing to human health protection while keeping the certainty attached to each case definition visible. A report of several cases is not proof that every contact in that workplace became infected.

sections.heading: Genetic similarity has greater resolution than an antibody label

paragraphs.text: Randolph and colleagues investigated 59 dogs associated with the 2021 Los Angeles outbreak. Fifty four survived to discharge, although some retained kidney abnormalities. Culture and genome analysis identified serovar Canicola in the characterized organisms, but the genomes were distinct. Exposure to indoor congregate facilities was associated with peak period cases; the limited postpeak genetic samples did not establish direct dog to dog transmission. This combination is instructive: the same serovar name does not mean two infections came from one identical source. A forensic or public health conclusion needs the clinical and sampling timeline, the resolution of the typing method and the alternatives supported by the investigation. The report identified no associated human cases. That observation does not establish zero zoonotic risk; it records the outcome of this investigation within its available surveillance and samples.

sections.heading: Protecting people while diagnosis is still being resolved

paragraphs.text: Leptospirosis is zoonotic, meaning it can pass between animals and people. CDC advises avoiding contact with urine or blood from an infected animal before appropriate treatment, using protective clothing when contact is unavoidable, covering skin wounds and washing hands after handling animals or potentially contaminated material. Owners should obtain the veterinarian's instructions for cleaning and for protecting other household animals. People concerned about an exposure should contact a healthcare professional and explain the animal contact, rather than assume a canine test supplies a human diagnosis. These precautions are relevant while the investigation is incomplete because recognition can lag behind illness. They should be proportionate and practical: the aim is to reduce contact with potentially infectious body fluids while the dog receives necessary care, not to infer that ordinary proximity proves transmission.

sections.heading: Prevention and diagnostic interpretation remain separate tasks

paragraphs.text: The American Veterinary Medical Association recommends vaccination against leptospirosis for dogs and reducing exposure to contaminated water, rodents and other possible sources. Vaccination also reduces the chance that an infected dog spreads the organism. The preventive plan is discussed with the veterinarian using the dog's record and local circumstances. Antibody testing after vaccination asks a different question from whether the dog currently needs treatment for leptospirosis. A positive antibody response can be an expected consequence of immunization; it should not be used to label the vaccine itself as an infection. Conversely, a vaccination record should remain available if illness develops, rather than being treated as a reason to skip examination. Preserve dates, product names, specimen results and follow up so that prevention and later diagnostic decisions can be interpreted together.

sections.heading: The clinical condition determines urgency

paragraphs.text: Cornell's canine guidance emphasizes that diagnosis needs both routine assessment and tests directed at Leptospira. A dog with repeated vomiting, jaundice, marked lethargy, reduced urine or breathing difficulty needs prompt veterinary attention; severe deterioration warrants emergency assessment. Owners should not wait for the next scheduled antibody sample before reporting a change. Routine blood work and urinalysis help establish organ damage and guide support, while PCR and antibody tests investigate the cause. A useful discussion asks which question each result answers, which specimen was tested, what treatment preceded collection and what remains uncertain. The immediate goal is to assess and support the animal, while the diagnostic record develops. A negative early test and a serious clinical problem can coexist, and both observations need attention.

content.name: Veterinary dermatophyte testing

hook.text: Does a positive ringworm test show infected hair, viable fungus, or fungal material merely carried on the coat?

sections.heading: Ringworm is a fungal diagnosis with several different kinds of evidence

paragraphs.text: Dermatophytosis, commonly called ringworm, is caused by fungi that use keratin, the structural material in hair, superficial skin and claws. It is not a worm infection. This chapter covers dogs and cats; studies in shelter cats do not automatically validate the same performance in every dog. The World Association for Veterinary Dermatology (WAVD) consensus found no single diagnostic gold standard. Examination and direct microscopy can demonstrate infected hair; culture grows recoverable fungus; polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detects selected fungal DNA, or genetic material. Each answers a different question. Disease can be contagious to other animals and people, so investigation and containment matter even when the pet seems otherwise well. A positive coat sample alone, however, does not establish tissue invasion, the source of infection or the appropriateness of prolonged isolation.

sections.heading: The organism, animal and exposure setting shape the suspicion

paragraphs.text: ESCCAP's superficial-mycosis guidance describes Microsporum canis and other dermatophytes affecting dogs and cats. Despite its name, M. canis is particularly important in cats. Some other dermatophytes are associated with soil or contact with other animal hosts. Young animals, damaged skin and crowded housing can influence risk, but no breed or housing label establishes the diagnosis. Hair loss, scaling, crusts and broken hairs can have several causes, including parasites, bacterial infection and other inflammatory disease. Ask about new animals, grooming equipment, previous treatment and people with skin lesions. These details guide sampling and household precautions; they do not prove who infected whom. The date a lesion was noticed is also not necessarily the date infection began.

sections.heading: A Wood lamp helps find hairs worth testing

paragraphs.text: A proper Wood lamp uses ultraviolet light to reveal characteristic fluorescence along some infected hair shafts. It is a clinical search tool: the veterinarian identifies suspect hairs, then examines or submits them. Merck's veterinary guidance emphasizes that no single test is definitive in every case. The relevant apple-green signal is in hair, not simply any glowing scale, lint or material on the surface. Equipment, examiner technique, the organism and previous therapy influence what is seen. A negative examination cannot exclude every dermatophyte infection, particularly infections with organisms that do not show the same fluorescence. Conversely, a glowing spot photographed with a household ultraviolet device is not enough to diagnose ringworm. The result needs the skin examination and confirmation appropriate to the presentation.

sections.heading: A shelter study measures the limits of lamp screening

paragraphs.text: A study of seventy shelter cats compared Wood lamp examination with fungal culture. Culture detected Microsporum canis in about sixty-four percent, while about forty-nine percent showed fluorescence. Relative to culture, the lamp examination had a reported sensitivity of seventy-one percent and specificity of ninety-two percent. Sensitivity is the proportion detected among reference-positive cats; specificity is correct exclusion among reference-negative cats. The figures support trained use at intake while showing that some cats will be missed. They are not universal properties of every lamp, examiner or animal population. A shelter with frequent infection also differs from a household where the starting probability is low. Screening can sort the next diagnostic step, but a negative light examination cannot by itself settle an exposed animal's status.

sections.heading: Direct microscopy connects the fungus to a particular hair

paragraphs.text: The clinician can examine selected hairs and skin material microscopically for fungal filaments and arthroconidia, the small fungal units that form around infected hairs. Recognizing the structures takes training; normal debris can be mistaken for infection. In an observer study using samples from ten infected and ten uninfected cats, veterinarians classified stained and unstained hairs before and after seeing illustrated guidance. Reference images improved accuracy, whereas staining alone did not provide the same benefit. The study's overall comparison with culture also showed imperfect sensitivity and specificity. Thus, microscopy is valuable evidence when recognizable fungal structures involve a compatible hair, but the apparent simplicity of looking down a microscope does not make interpretation automatic. Discordant results should prompt review of the specimen and the clinical picture.

sections.heading: Dermoscopy can locate abnormal hairs without identifying every infection

paragraphs.text: Dermoscopy magnifies the skin and hair surface. In a study of sixty-seven cats, investigators compared this examination with fungal culture. Thirty-six cats had culture-confirmed dermatophytes, including several species; dermoscopy was positive in twenty-one of those thirty-six. Characteristic bent or comma-like hairs can therefore help a clinician choose hairs for further testing, but the method missed a substantial portion of culture-positive cats. This is a diagnostic aid, not a substitute for species identification or a universal negative screen. Its value is practical: an examination directed toward abnormal hairs may improve the material sent for microscopy and culture. The appearance of a damaged hair alone cannot distinguish every fungus from other processes that break or distort hair shafts.

sections.heading: A red culture medium is not a species identification

paragraphs.text: Dermatophyte test medium, abbreviated DTM, changes color under conditions that can accompany fungal growth. The colony must still be assessed, often microscopically, to identify the organism. In a blinded multicenter study, hair from fifty-four dogs and forty-seven cats with suspected disease, plus nine healthy controls, was compared between clinic testing and a mycology laboratory. Referral clinicians who examined colony appearance and microscopy achieved much closer agreement with the laboratory than general-practice readers relying only on color change. The groups differed in who read the plates and how, so the result should not be reduced to a judgment about all practices. It demonstrates that a culture is an interpreted laboratory process, not simply a container that turns red when ringworm is present.

sections.heading: Culture timing depends on growth, treatment and laboratory conditions

paragraphs.text: Stuntebeck and colleagues reviewed 13,772 feline fungal cultures, of which 2,876 grew Microsporum canis. Only seventy-six positive cultures required more than fourteen days for recovery or confirmation. Late positives were more frequent among samples from treated cats, where growth and microscopic features could be altered. These were culture specimens, not 13,772 independent cats. The study supports a laboratory-specific approach to finalizing cultures and avoiding unnecessary waiting, while acknowledging that a highly experienced research laboratory may differ from a clinic. A preliminary no-growth report is not the same as the laboratory's final negative result. Treatment history matters because antifungal exposure can suppress or distort growth; collection and interpretation should follow the veterinarian's and laboratory's plan rather than a fixed household countdown.

sections.heading: Positive coat cultures can include mechanical carriers

paragraphs.text: A Northwestern US shelter study distinguished infected cats from cats carrying small quantities of fungus on the coat. In the study population of 11,214 admitted cats, 202 were diagnosed with Microsporum canis infection and nineteen were classified as fomite carriers. A fomite is contaminated material; on an animal, carriage can mean that fungal particles are present without established hair infection. Lamp performance and culture timing varied within this setting, and kittens and transported cats had different risks. These findings show why the examination, colony burden, repeat samples and exposure context belong together. A colony count is useful information under a defined protocol, not an independent universal threshold that can classify every pet. The same positive culture label can conceal biologically different situations.

sections.heading: PCR can stay positive after cultures have become negative

paragraphs.text: Jacobson and colleagues compared a commercial PCR panel with culture in 132 shelter cats. All twenty-eight initially culture-positive cats were PCR positive, but PCR was also positive in twelve initially culture-negative cats; repeat cultures subsequently identified infection in two of the rechecked cats. Monitoring data from seventeen treated cats were especially instructive: fourteen remained PCR positive at the first negative culture and eleven at the second. PCR detects DNA and can detect nonviable fungal material or coat contamination, so positivity after treatment does not automatically mean continuing active disease. The observed results are specific to this assay and population. A negative PCR was reassuring in this study, but interpreting cure still requires clinical findings and the agreed monitoring method rather than indefinite treatment for residual DNA.

sections.heading: Another PCR study found missed infections as well as false positives

paragraphs.text: A Western Canadian retrospective study selected 246 animals with sufficient paired records: 198 cats and forty-eight dogs. Against a culture-based reference incorporating colony scoring, combined PCR sensitivity was about eighty-six percent and specificity about ninety-five percent. Seventy-two animals were culture positive. Those results differ from the smaller study reporting no PCR false negatives. Differences in specimens, pathogen targets, reference definitions and population can explain such variation; accuracy is not a permanent property of the word PCR. The 246 selected animals also should not be confused with the 125,939 total shelter admissions during the study period. A clinician facing a compatible lesion and a negative PCR can therefore consider culture or another assessment instead of assuming that molecular testing has excluded all dermatophytes.

sections.heading: Excellent results in a small study need their population attached

paragraphs.text: A separate 2024 investigation compared dermoscopy, direct hair examination, several culture media and PCR using forty-eight feline samples. PCR performed best within that study, whereas direct examination and dermoscopy were less satisfactory. That finding is useful evidence for the evaluated workflow, but it does not erase the imperfect PCR performance observed in larger shelter datasets. Small selected samples provide limited information about uncommon errors, and comparison methods can themselves miss infection or detect carriage. When a laboratory advertises high accuracy, ask which animals and organisms were tested, how infection was defined and whether treatment had begun. A sensible diagnostic plan can use a rapid result while retaining another method for a mismatch between the laboratory report and the animal's lesions.

sections.heading: Unusual nodules may require investigation below the hair coat

paragraphs.text: Most routine ringworm involves superficial structures, but deep, nodular or draining lesions require a different diagnostic approach. The European Advisory Board on Cat Diseases (ABCD) guidance recommends cytology or biopsy with appropriate fungal stains for atypical feline lesions. Cytology examines individual cells and material; histopathology examines tissue architecture and can show whether fungal structures occur within an inflammatory lesion. The laboratory needs to know that dermatophytosis is being considered so that suitable stains and cultures are requested. A coat culture alone cannot establish what caused a deep mass. Conversely, a negative superficial sample cannot reliably explain away an abnormal nodule. These are veterinary procedures chosen for the patient, with attention to other infections and tumors. Worsening, painful, ulcerated or extensive disease deserves assessment rather than repeated home surface checks.

sections.heading: Two real canine kerion cases reached documented cure

paragraphs.text: A 2026 report described a five-year-old Silky Terrier and an eight-year-old Shetland Sheepdog with inflammatory lesions called kerions. These raised lesions can resemble bacterial infection or a tumor rather than a familiar ring of hair loss. Hair microscopy and culture demonstrated Microsporum canis, and DNA sequencing supported species identification. After veterinary systemic and topical treatment, the Terrier had clinical cure by day eighty-one, with mycological cure, meaning no further recoverable fungus on follow-up testing, confirmed fifteen days later. The Sheepdog's lesion had resolved with hair regrowth by day sixty, and the report describes subsequent mycological cure. These outcomes distinguish improved appearance from follow-up evidence about fungus. Similar lesions in household members were reported, but that history alone cannot prove the precise direction or source of transmission.

sections.heading: A deep feline infection improved temporarily and then had a fatal outcome

paragraphs.text: A 2024 report described a three-year-old Korean domestic shorthair cat with chronic crusts and ulcerated nodules. Cytology showed fungal filaments; tissue examination demonstrated a deep inflammatory process containing fungal plaques, and culture identified Microsporum canis alongside Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis was dermatophytic pseudomycetoma, a deep mass of fungal and inflammatory material, with secondary bacterial skin infection. Several veterinary treatments produced partial improvement, but substantial nodules remained, lesions later recurred and the cat died ten months after presentation. The report does not establish a necropsy-proven mechanism of death or a fatal prognosis for ordinary superficial ringworm. Its lesson is that depth, recurrence and concurrent infection change the investigation and prognosis, and that early improvement is not the same outcome as sustained resolution.

sections.heading: Other deep infections have resolved, with follow-up qualifications

paragraphs.text: An earlier report described a Persian cat and a Maine Coon with generalized dermatophytosis and dermatophyte mycetomas. Culture identified Microsporum canis. Initial itraconazole was ineffective in one cat and poorly tolerated in the other. Following a revised veterinary plan, both achieved clinical and mycological cure, with sequential negative cultures reached after fourteen and twelve weeks, respectively. The Persian also underwent removal of the residual nodule. Its generalized skin disease later recurred after treatment stopped and was managed with intermittent treatment; the Maine Coon's nodule had resolved medically. These are different individual courses within one report, not two uncomplicated permanent cures. They demonstrate why adverse effects, lesion depth, culture results and recurrence must all be preserved when discussing an apparent treatment success.

sections.heading: A real shelter controlled disease while continuing adoptions

paragraphs.text: An open-admission shelter field study combined trained intake examinations, culture, separation of risk groups, treatment and changes in animal flow. Dermatophytosis was eliminated from the public adoption area within five months while admissions and adoptions continued. Of 273 culture-positive new admissions during one eight-month period, only sixty had the combined lesion, lamp and microscopy findings of true infection; the other 213 were judged mechanical carriers after follow-up. Disease later reappeared with cats returning from foster care, but the investigators could not determine where those cats originally became infected. The response illustrates the welfare value of distinguishing carriage from disease and protecting unexposed animals. It does not establish that every positive culture requires the same treatment or that a returning foster household caused transmission.

sections.heading: Hoarding investigations require examination alongside cultures

paragraphs.text: Researchers reviewing four large cat seizures screened for dermatophytosis in one investigation. Among seventy-six cats with suspicious skin lesions, sixty-nine grew Microsporum canis; approximately half were considered truly infected and half mechanical carriers. The selected lesional group is not a prevalence estimate for every seized cat or every multi-cat household. It is a particularly useful forensic example because even in a documented welfare investigation the culture result did not establish the same biological state in every animal. A defensible individual record retains lesion descriptions, photographs, identification, sampling dates, microscopy and repeat findings alongside environmental and care evidence. A positive ringworm result alone cannot establish neglect, the duration of suffering, who introduced an infection or whether an owner knew about it.

sections.heading: Skin lesions are common enough that appearance alone can mislead

paragraphs.text: An Ontario surveillance study sampled four hundred cats admitted to three shelters during a defined winter-to-spring period. None yielded dermatophytes, although seventy-seven had skin lesions and many samples grew other fungi. Positive laboratory control cultures grew as expected. This does not prove that those shelters or that region can never have ringworm: only one period and a few facilities were sampled, and no method has perfect sensitivity. It does show that visible skin disease is not synonymous with dermatophytosis and that background frequency varies greatly between settings. An outbreak response should be proportional to confirmed findings and exposure evidence. Proper testing protects animals both from missed contagious disease and from unnecessary treatment, confinement or disruption based only on nonspecific hair loss.

sections.heading: Treatment studies need a clear definition of cure

paragraphs.text: A 2025 randomized shelter-cat trial compared three topical approaches while all cats received oral itraconazole. The analysis included seventy-six cats and defined success as mycological cure by seven weeks. All lime-sulfur-group cats reached that endpoint; some cats in the alternative shampoo groups did not. Average cure times were shorter with lime sulfur, although the prespecified statistical test of the alternatives' inferiority remained inconclusive because confidence intervals, the estimated uncertainty ranges, crossed its margin. It compares combined treatment programs in cats, not topical products used alone or owner-selected substitutes. Veterinary monitoring also considers tolerance and temperature during bathing. The clinically relevant question is how the animal and viable fungal burden are changing under a supervised plan.

sections.heading: Environmental contamination is manageable and does not make a home hopeless

paragraphs.text: A laundering study tested fabrics contaminated experimentally and through contact with infected kittens. Naturally exposed towels and denim frequently retained small amounts of recoverable fungus after one wash, but none was detected after two washes under the tested conditions. The study demonstrates the importance of mechanical removal and adequate washing rather than assuming that every contaminated washable item must be discarded. Its exact findings belong to those fabrics, machines and protocols; they are not proof that any quick wash sterilizes every household material. The veterinary team can adapt cleaning to the setting and vulnerable household members. Keep contaminated hair and laundry contained during transport, preserve normal animal care and enrichment, and avoid turning environmental test results into a requirement for impossible whole-house sterility.

sections.heading: Cleaning and repeat testing should answer a defined clinical question

paragraphs.text: An experimental disinfectant study compared eight commercial products against spores from cat hair. All inhibited growth in a simple suspension test, but performance on contaminated textile surfaces depended on how thoroughly the product was applied. A laboratory fungicidal claim therefore does not mean that a light application over hair and debris will achieve the same result. Cleaning removes material; a suitable disinfectant acts on what remains, under its labeled conditions and veterinary advice. Do not improvise mixtures or apply environmental products to the animal. In practice, the useful endpoint is a recovering pet with a coherent examination and testing record, together with manageable transmission precautions. Repeating a coat PCR without deciding how its result will change care can prolong uncertainty instead of resolving it.
