content.name: Veterinary skin scraping and surface cytology

hook.text: A few cells or mites can redirect an itchy animal’s care. The sample’s site and depth determine what the microscope can reveal—and what it can miss.

sections.heading: Start with the animal, then examine the slide

paragraphs.text: Skin scraping collects material for microscopic examination, often to look for mites. Surface cytology collects cells and associated material to investigate inflammation, bacteria, yeasts or abnormal tissue cells. In dogs and cats, many different diseases cause similar redness, crusts, hair loss or itching, so neither test replaces a history and full examination. The veterinarian asks where the problem began, whether itching preceded the lesions, which treatments were used, whether other animals are affected, and whether there has been travel or recent bathing. These details help select a useful lesion and explain unexpected findings. A photograph of a rash may identify a pattern, but it cannot show whether mites or intracellular bacteria are present.

sections.heading: Basic tests come before an allergy label

paragraphs.text: The American Animal Hospital Association’s 2023 guidance recommends a minimum dermatologic database: a basic set of observations and samples, including flea combing, skin cytology and appropriate scrapings, with ear cytology when ear disease is present. The selection in cats is guided by the pattern of lesions as well as the history. Parasites, secondary bacterial infection and yeast disease can produce or intensify itching, including in an animal that also has an allergy. Finding and managing them helps clarify what remains. A skin scraping is not an allergy test, and a negative scraping does not establish allergy. Rechecking after initial care is part of the diagnostic process because different causes can coexist or become apparent over time.

sections.heading: Tape, impressions and swabs collect different material

paragraphs.text: An impression preparation transfers material from an accessible moist or draining lesion onto a glass slide. A swab can transfer discharge from a fold or other moist site to a slide. These approaches are usually quick, but their usefulness depends on the material that actually reaches the microscope. An impression of an ulcer surface may show inflammation and surface microbes while missing the deeper cause. The veterinary team chooses the method to match the lesion rather than assuming that every sample called “cytology” is equivalent.

Adhesive tape collects superficial material such as scales, cells and organisms. It can help recover some surface-dwelling mites and is a different specimen from a deep scraping. The target organism’s location therefore matters when choosing between tape, hair examination and scraping.

sections.heading: Depth follows the suspected parasite’s habitat

paragraphs.text: The European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites, abbreviated ESCCAP, distinguishes surface sampling from methods that reach hair follicles. The epidermis is the outer skin layer; its outermost keratin layer contains flattened, dead cells. Some mites occupy this surface region, while follicular Demodex mites live deeper around hair roots and associated glands. A superficial sample suited to a surface-dwelling mite may therefore miss follicular disease. A trichogram, meaning microscopic examination of collected hairs and their roots, can provide another route to follicular material in selected sites. Sampling is a professional procedure with depth and location chosen for the animal and suspected disease; the explanation is not a recommendation for owners to scrape irritated skin at home.

sections.heading: Preparation errors can hide or imitate findings

paragraphs.text: A useful cytology sample needs enough well-preserved material spread so individual cells can be assessed. Thick debris, cell rupture, poor drying or staining problems can obscure the very structures being sought. Routine stains colour nuclei and cytoplasm differently, making cell types and small organisms easier to recognize. Cornell University’s eClinpath guidance also stresses the vulnerability of slides to formalin fumes: slides submitted near a formalin-preserved biopsy can acquire staining artifacts and become difficult to interpret. An impression can yield only surface contamination rather than representative lesional tissue. The receiving laboratory needs the animal’s history and precise sampling site, because a technically readable slide can still answer the wrong clinical question if its origin is unclear.

sections.heading: Inflammatory cells are clues rather than a complete diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Neutrophils are white blood cells commonly recruited to acute inflammation and many bacterial infections. Macrophages are cells that engulf material and can become prominent in longer-standing inflammation or responses to foreign material and some infections. Eosinophils can occur with parasites and hypersensitivity, among other causes. Their relative abundance helps describe a reaction pattern but does not uniquely identify its cause. Even neutrophils that look swollen or damaged are not absolute proof of bacterial infection: preservation artifacts, fungi and chemical irritation can produce overlapping changes. Conversely, neutrophils that look relatively normal do not exclude bacteria. The observer searches for organisms, their relationship to cells and the wider pattern before attaching a disease name to the sample.

sections.heading: Bacteria: being present and causing pyoderma are different

paragraphs.text: Pyoderma means bacterial skin infection. The International Society for Companion Animal Infectious Diseases, or ISCAID, recommends cytology in suspected canine pyoderma. Cocci are round bacteria and rods are elongated bacteria; these shapes guide interpretation but do not name a species. Bacteria engulfed within inflammatory cells provide stronger support for infection than a few organisms lying outside cells on otherwise healthy skin. Extracellular bacteria accompanied by damaged-cell material can also be important, and substantial bacterial overgrowth on an inflamed lesion may occur without obvious inflammatory cells. No universal bacterial-count threshold has been validated for every site and method. A negative surface preparation also has limited ability to rule out infection deeper in the skin.

sections.heading: Microscopy does not supply an antibiotic susceptibility result

paragraphs.text: Round bacteria on a slide cannot distinguish a susceptible staphylococcus from a resistant one. Culture identifies organisms capable of growing under the laboratory’s conditions, while antimicrobial susceptibility testing assesses their response to selected drugs. These results require interpretation alongside the lesion and cytology because colonizing bacteria may also grow. The World Association for Veterinary Dermatology’s guidance on meticillin-resistant staphylococci distinguishes colonization from infection and emphasizes reliable species identification and resistance testing. Detecting a resistant organism does not by itself mean that disease is more severe or untreatable. For deep or persistent disease, the veterinarian chooses a specimen that represents the affected tissue; a casual surface swab can misdirect treatment toward an incidental organism.

sections.heading: Yeast counts belong in clinical context

paragraphs.text: Malassezia yeasts, often recognizable as small oval or budding cells, can inhabit healthy canine and feline skin. They can also overgrow or contribute to inflammation when the skin environment changes. The World Association for Veterinary Dermatology, abbreviated WAVD, recommends interpreting lesional cytology together with compatible signs and response to appropriate care. Anatomical site, breed, sampling technique and the animal’s immune response affect the meaning of a count. Some sensitive animals can have important disease with relatively few yeasts, while detecting yeasts alone does not establish dermatitis. A report should therefore describe the method, approximate abundance and inflammatory context. The aim is to explain the animal’s sore or itchy skin rather than to sterilize a normally inhabited surface.

sections.heading: A thirty-dog study shows why the method changes the count

paragraphs.text: Rich and colleagues compared three cytology collection techniques in thirty client-owned dogs with atopic dermatitis and lesions consistent with bacterial or Malassezia skin disease. In the blinded comparison, a preparation suspending collected surface debris yielded an average of 12.7 more bacteria per evaluated sample than impression smears and 13.5 more than tape preparations. Tape detected slightly more Malassezia than the suspension method, averaging 0.22 additional organisms per sample. These were method-comparison outcomes, not evidence that one technique cured disease or was best for every lesion. The studied dogs were a selected clinical population. The practical implication is that an apparent change in microbial burden can partly reflect how material was collected and counted.

sections.heading: Demodex in dogs and cats: the species distinction matters

paragraphs.text: The Companion Animal Parasite Council, CAPC, describes different Demodex species and habitats. Canine Demodex canis inhabits hair follicles; excessive proliferation is associated with demodicosis. In cats, Demodex cati also occupies follicles, whereas Demodex gatoi lives superficially and can be contagious between cats. Grooming can remove surface mites, making them difficult to recover even from an itchy cat. Deep scrapings, hair examination and tape preparations therefore have different roles depending on the suspected species. In occasional difficult cases, a biopsy reveals mites despite negative earlier samples. Finding a mite can establish an important part of the diagnosis, but its species and location matter; the label “Demodex positive” alone leaves clinically relevant information unresolved.

sections.heading: The condition that allowed mites to multiply may need investigation

paragraphs.text: WAVD’s 2020 demodicosis consensus recommends looking for predisposing conditions when disease begins in adult dogs or cats. Immune suppression can arise from illness or medication, and an underlying cause is not always found even after investigation. The examination should therefore extend beyond the visible patches when the history warrants it. Improvement is assessed both clinically and through repeat sampling: hair regrowth or reduced redness can precede elimination of the abnormal mite population. Rechecks compare the same previously affected areas and the numbers and developmental stages recovered. A negative sample is valuable evidence of response, but its interpretation depends on the sites sampled, the method and previous findings rather than appearance alone.

sections.heading: Eight young dogs: early negative hair samples missed remaining mites

paragraphs.text: A 2019 pilot study by Barillas and colleagues followed eight dogs with juvenile generalized demodicosis. It compared deep skin scraping, microscopic hair examination and a veterinary tape-impression technique that also obtained follicular material. Hair examination recovered fewer mites during much of treatment. At week two, three dogs had negative hair examinations while mites remained detectable by the other techniques. By week four, two dogs were negative on scraping but positive on tape, while one showed the reverse mismatch. From week five to the study’s end, all techniques were negative for mite life stages. The endpoint was microscopic monitoring during that small study, not proof of lifelong cure. It demonstrates why one negative method should not prematurely end follow-up.

sections.heading: Two Finnish cats: diagnosis and follow-up stayed household-specific

paragraphs.text: Saari and colleagues reported Demodex gatoi in ten cats from six Finnish households containing twenty-one cats altogether. In household three, a two-year-old Exotic male and a three-year-old neutered Persian male had itching, hair loss and scaling, with mites recovered from superficial samples. Initial regimens were unsuccessful; a later veterinarian-directed regimen was rated effective using clinical examination and scraping, with twenty-four months of follow-up recorded. The historical treatment details are not current prescribing instructions. In a different household, all six cats remained symptomless despite mites being found on one cat. These observations separate an identified parasite from the severity of disease in every contact animal. Household examination and response helped interpretation; a positive cat did not establish when or from whom transmission occurred.

sections.heading: Sarcoptic mange can remain plausible after negative scrapings

paragraphs.text: Sarcoptes mites cause canine scabies, an often intensely itchy, contagious infestation. Characteristic distribution, possible exposure and itching in contact animals can support suspicion, but allergic and other skin diseases can resemble it. Merck Veterinary Manual describes the difficulty of confirming some cases because scrapings can be negative. The veterinarian assesses the whole pattern rather than interpreting “no mites seen” as a universal exclusion. When suspicion remains high, further sampling or a professionally supervised diagnostic treatment trial may be appropriate. That trial still requires clinical reassessment: improvement can be influenced by concurrent infections and other treatment. People with an associated rash should seek their own medical advice instead of using an animal’s parasiticide.

sections.heading: Scale on the coat can require a different search

paragraphs.text: Cheyletiella mites are associated with scaling often most apparent along the back, while Lynxacarus mites in cats cling to hair shafts. These nonburrowing parasites may be recovered through combinations of coat examination, combed debris, tape or microscopic hair assessment. Their eggs and attachment patterns can also help identification. A laboratory finding of “scale only” does not automatically exclude them if the sampled area or technique was unsuitable. CAPC notes that combining appropriate techniques can improve recovery. The appearance commonly called walking dandruff is a clue to investigate, not a reliable visual diagnosis for an owner. Finding a coat parasite also does not rule out a separate bacterial or yeast complication on damaged skin.

sections.heading: Mange findings do not establish neglect or a transmission history

paragraphs.text: Feline scabies caused by Notoedres cati commonly begins around the head and ears and can produce marked crusting and itching. CAPC describes confirmation by identifying the mite in skin scrapings and notes that grooming can also lead to mites being recovered on fecal examination. These are findings about an infestation, rather than a complete history of how it developed. A scraping can document organisms at a sampled site; it cannot alone establish how long an animal was affected, who transmitted them, what care was previously attempted, or whether a person neglected the animal. A welfare investigation needs the clinical course, physical condition, records and circumstances alongside the test. Visible suffering requires care while those questions are investigated.

sections.heading: A thirteen-dog study: DNA remained detectable after other findings fell

paragraphs.text: Díaz and colleagues studied thirteen dogs: eleven with Malassezia-associated paw inflammation and two healthy controls. Multiple sites produced fifteen pretreatment diseased samples, three healthy samples and four post-treatment samples from three affected dogs. Thus twenty-two samples did not represent twenty-two independent animals. The diseased samples had higher yeast counts and culture growth. After antifungal treatment, the four repeat samples showed very low or absent yeasts by cytology and no culture growth, while yeast DNA remained detectable by quantitative polymerase chain reaction, or qPCR. This small study compared measurement methods and selected repeat samples; it did not establish a universal molecular threshold for cure. A DNA signal alone could not demonstrate ongoing clinically important dermatitis.

sections.heading: Detached skin cells can suggest an immune-mediated disease

paragraphs.text: Keratinocytes are the main cells of the epidermis. Acantholysis means that these cells have lost their normal attachments and rounded up separately. Seeing numerous acantholytic cells with inflammation can suggest pemphigus foliaceus, an immune-mediated blistering and crusting disease. However, the finding is not uniquely diagnostic: some bacterial or fungal pustular diseases can produce overlapping changes. Guidance presented at the World Small Animal Veterinary Association congress emphasizes this distinction. The veterinarian considers fresh lesions, organisms, response to previous care and, when needed, biopsy before prescribing immune-suppressing treatment. Suppressing the immune system because a slide merely resembles pemphigus could worsen an unrecognized infection. A descriptive cytology finding should therefore remain separate from the final disease diagnosis.

sections.heading: Thirty-five cats with pemphigus: control did not mean permanent cure

paragraphs.text: Bizikova and Burrows reported an original series of thirty-five cats with pemphigus foliaceus, separately from their literature review. All thirty-five had acantholysis confirmed by cytology, and twenty-four also had histological confirmation. Disease control was achieved in thirty-one, with a median time of twenty-two days; control meant that new lesions stopped forming and existing active lesions largely or completely healed. Flare-ups occurred in twenty-four of those thirty-one cats. The original cohort’s median follow-up was fifteen months. This outcome supports a treatable disease while showing why a one-time improvement or slide cannot establish permanent recovery. The report’s original thirty-five-cat outcomes should not be merged with its larger reviewed collection of previously published cats.

sections.heading: When surface samples cannot answer the question

paragraphs.text: A skin biopsy preserves tissue architecture: the arrangement of layers, follicles, glands and inflammatory changes. Texas A&M’s dermatology service describes its use after initial tests when immune-mediated disease, follicular disorders, deep infection or cancer remain concerns. Several lesions may need sampling because an old ulcer and a fresh lesion can reveal different information. Local anaesthesia, sedation or general anaesthesia may be appropriate depending on the site and animal, with pain and anxiety addressed explicitly. A superficial sample showing only inflammation is not necessarily a failed test; it may correctly reveal that the surface cannot distinguish among deeper causes. Persistent, unusual or worsening lesions call for reassessment rather than repeating the same inadequate specimen indefinitely.

sections.heading: A negative routine slide does not exclude ringworm

paragraphs.text: Dermatophytosis, often called ringworm, is fungal infection of keratinized tissue such as hair and superficial skin. It is different from Malassezia overgrowth, and routine bacterial or yeast cytology is not a complete dermatophyte work-up. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals shelter guidance uses the clinical picture together with appropriate Wood’s lamp examination, direct hair assessment, fungal culture or molecular testing. A Wood’s lamp is a specialized ultraviolet examination, not proof that every glowing substance is infected hair. In shelters, the distinction matters because unnecessary isolation consumes care capacity while missed infection can spread. The veterinarian chooses additional fungal testing when the lesion pattern and exposure warrant it, despite an unrevealing routine surface slide.

sections.heading: Painful deep disease changes the urgency

paragraphs.text: Deep pyoderma can produce painful swelling, ulceration, crusts and draining tracts releasing blood or pus. These lesions deserve prompt veterinary attention, particularly if the animal is also lethargic, feverish, eating poorly or deteriorating. MSD Veterinary Manual distinguishes deep disease from surface and superficial infection and notes that recurrent deep disease in cats can accompany systemic illness or unusual infections. Surface microscopy alone cannot establish the full extent of such disease. The immediate priorities are comfort, assessment of the animal’s overall condition, and representative diagnostic material. A report of a few surface bacteria should not delay care for a painful deep lesion, and persistent redness should not automatically trigger repeated antibiotics without reviewing the underlying diagnosis.

sections.heading: Make the result reproducible and useful at the next visit

paragraphs.text: Record species, sampling site, lesion type, previous treatment and response. Include clinical context and previous results, so later clinicians can interpret the sampled finding.

content.name: Equine fecal egg count
content.hook: Why can a horse shed no detectable parasite eggs yet still have serious parasitic disease?

sections.heading: What the number actually measures

paragraphs.text: An equine fecal egg count, usually shortened to FEC, estimates parasite eggs per gram of manure, or EPG. It is chiefly a tool for monitoring egg shedding and checking the effect of deworming medicines, called anthelmintics. The 2024 guideline from the American Association of Equine Practitioners, or AAEP, emphasizes that the count does not measure the number of worms inside the horse or diagnose the cause of disease. The distinction is central to safe interpretation. This chapter concerns horses. Results and management rules should not automatically be transferred to donkeys, zebras, ruminants or people.

A long Swedish monitoring programme shows why individual testing can help pasture management. Researchers analyzed 43,330 submitted samples from 26,625 horses on 935 premises. In that selected programme, 26 percent of horses accounted for 80 percent of total strongyle egg output. Egg shedding was therefore unevenly distributed: treating every horse as an identical contributor would miss useful information. Yet an adult horse's category was not permanent. Among 1,034 horses examined in three consecutive years, 62 percent stayed in the same low or high category using the study's 200 EPG division. These findings describe a monitored population and its definitions. They do not establish that a fixed minority always sheds the same proportion on every farm.

sections.heading: From fresh manure to a microscopic estimate

paragraphs.text: The sample should belong to an identified horse, with its collection time and recent treatment history recorded. Old manure from a shared paddock introduces uncertainty before the microscope is used. Storage can then change recovery. Crawley and colleagues tested horse manure stored under different conditions: counts remained comparatively stable during a week of refrigeration but declined after longer refrigeration, and tested chemical fixatives also reduced recovery. Their findings do not mean every specimen can wait a week without consequence. Arrange prompt delivery and follow the laboratory's requirements. Freezing or adding a preservative without its advice can make results difficult to compare with the validated method or an earlier sample.

In a flotation method, the laboratory mixes measured manure with a liquid that helps parasite eggs separate from heavier material, then examines a known portion. A multiplication factor converts the eggs actually seen into EPG. As a purely hypothetical arithmetic example, four eggs seen with a factor of 50 gives 200 EPG; four eggs seen is not a claim that only four eggs existed in the whole sample. A 2024 comparison of manual and automated methods emphasized that the factor describes theoretical counting resolution, not guaranteed clinical sensitivity. Egg losses during processing still matter. A method reporting increments of 50 cannot reliably distinguish all small differences within those increments.

McMaster chambers, Mini FLOTAC and centrifugation-based approaches use different sample volumes and processing steps. In a Cornell laboratory comparison, researchers used standardized microscopic beads to study recovery and then examined strongyle eggs in samples from 40 horses. Different methods did not become numerically interchangeable merely because all reported EPG. The bead work was a laboratory model, not proof that every type of parasite egg behaves identically. Accuracy describes closeness to the true amount, whereas precision describes agreement among repeated measurements. A consistently repeated underestimate can look precise while still being inaccurate. When comparing results over time, keep the method and laboratory visible alongside the number.

Thorough mixing, or homogenization, is necessary because the tiny portion examined must represent the larger specimen. An experiment comparing equine strongylid homogenization approaches investigated how preparation affected count magnitude and precision. This is a useful reminder that an EPG report is the end of a chain: sample selection, suspension, egg recovery, subsampling, recognition and multiplication. The result is not generated by photographing every egg in an entire bowel movement. Small changes around a management boundary may reflect measurement variation as well as changing biology. A veterinarian can ask the laboratory about repeatability or repeat an appropriate specimen before interpreting an unexpected difference as treatment failure.

sections.heading: Changing hosts seasons and parasite stages

paragraphs.text: Repeated counts in naturally infected horses show real variation within a horse as well as between horses. A longitudinal study reported only moderate overall repeatability, rather than perfect constancy. That does not make monitoring pointless: a pattern across appropriately timed samples can be informative even though each value varies. The practical interpretation is to retain the sequence of dates, not just the largest recorded number. A decrease after treatment should be judged with its starting count, method and sampling interval. Two reports from different dates cannot be compared as though they were duplicate measurements of the same material taken at the same moment.

Longitudinal work in five conservation pony populations examined individual shedding consistency, age effects and seasonal changes. It supports considering the host and environment when interpreting a series. Young horses are not simply small versions of established adult low shedders, and local grazing conditions affect exposure to infectious stages. Seasonal differences in egg output also should not be mistaken for a season when microscopy becomes inherently valid or invalid. A low count in winter does not certify that hidden stages are absent. The veterinarian combines repeated measurements with age, grazing history and local parasite biology to decide what monitoring is useful, rather than assigning a lifelong category from a single test.

Adult egg production is only one part of a parasite's life cycle. Routine egg counts miss migrating larvae and encysted larvae of small strongyles, also called cyathostomins, in the intestinal wall. Pinworm eggs are usually deposited around the anus rather than uniformly in manure; tapeworm detection has additional limitations. AAEP also rejects watery diarrheal specimens for quantitative FEC interpretation, although qualitative examinations may still be useful. A sick horse therefore needs clinical assessment even after a low or zero count. New colic, severe diarrhea, weakness or rapid deterioration warrants prompt veterinary contact rather than waiting for a routine monitoring result.

sections.heading: Species identification changes the question

paragraphs.text: Strongyle-type eggs look too similar for a routine count to reliably distinguish small strongyles from the more pathogenic large strongyle Strongylus vulgaris. Larval culture allows eggs to develop and a trained observer to identify later stages. A species-specific PCR instead detects selected DNA. Nielsen and colleagues developed a quantitative PCR for S vulgaris and compared it with traditional approaches on Danish farms. This provides identification beyond a generic egg count, but a fecal test still samples material being shed. It does not directly visualize immature parasites migrating within blood vessels, and a negative result cannot answer every question about past infection or tissue damage.

A German method comparison screened samples from 501 horses by S vulgaris PCR and used larval culture on a subset. In 321 directly comparable samples, including follow-up samples, PCR identified eleven positive samples and culture four. Those are sample counts, not eleven independent affected horses. The findings showed that the methods could disagree and that PCR detected more positives in that investigation. They do not mean a PCR result measures the number of worms or proves that a horse's colic is due to this organism. The question asked, the parasite stage and the clinical findings still limit the conclusion.

Pooling manure from several horses can reduce laboratory workload, but it changes the question from an individual's status to detection in the combined material. A study of pooled S vulgaris testing compared PCR with larval culture and found performance depended on how positive material was represented in the pool. Dilution can matter when one horse contributes a small amount of target among several others. A negative pooled result therefore does not provide the same evidence as suitable individual testing of every horse. Keep the identities and proportions in a pool documented. If an individual clinical or movement decision is required, the veterinarian should choose a sampling plan that actually resolves that individual question.

A Swedish hospital case-control study compared parasite investigations in horses with and without gastrointestinal disease. S vulgaris PCR positivity was 5.5 percent, while antibody evidence of exposure was much more frequent, at 62 percent. These tests were looking at different biological signals, not giving two interchangeable prevalence estimates. Antibodies reflect an immune response and fecal PCR identifies DNA in the sample. Horses with peritonitis had higher antibody levels, but that association did not assign the cause of every illness. The study reinforces why a general strongyle EPG number, a species-specific fecal test and a blood antibody result cannot simply be substituted for one another.

sections.heading: Tapeworms and complementary tests

paragraphs.text: Tapeworm segments release eggs unevenly, so an ordinary fecal egg count can miss infection. Antibody tests in saliva or serum provide a different signal. Lightbody and colleagues validated a saliva ELISA, an antibody-binding laboratory assay, using samples matched to tapeworm counts at an abattoir. In that study it detected at least one tapeworm with 83 percent sensitivity and 85 percent specificity. Neither value was perfect. This was a particular assay validated in horses, and the work was conducted by researchers affiliated with its developer. It does not validate every saliva test, prove that a positive animal's current colic is caused by tapeworms or authorize direct transfer to other equids.

A 2023 field investigation reported apparent treatment failure against equine tapeworms. The authors used egg detection before and after treatment while emphasizing the statistical difficulties of variable shedding and small groups. It is a warning against assuming that a familiar product must always work, but apparent failure is not automatically a standardized resistance diagnosis for every parasite. A negative post-treatment tapeworm specimen may arise because no eggs entered the aliquot examined. Conversely, repeated positive results can justify further investigation. Interpret the observations for the studied farm and method, retaining uncertainty rather than translating one publication into a claim that all tapeworm treatment has become ineffective.

sections.heading: Checking whether a treatment worked

paragraphs.text: The fecal egg count reduction test, or FECRT, compares appropriately timed counts before and after treatment in the same group. The 2023 guideline from the World Association for the Advancement of Veterinary Parasitology, or WAAVP, emphasizes enough actual eggs counted, suitable group sizes and statistical uncertainty. A hypothetical group mean falling from 500 to 25 EPG represents a 95 percent reduction, calculated as 100 times the difference divided by the starting mean. That arithmetic is not by itself a resistance verdict. Expected efficacy and interpretation depend on drug class, parasite and confidence limits. Wide limits mean the evidence is imprecise. A result near a boundary may remain inconclusive rather than being forced into effective or resistant.

The importance of checking locally is illustrated by a 2024 investigation on Irish farms. The authors found poor efficacy for some commonly used treatments, with reported fenbendazole reductions ranging from zero to 86.2 percent on affected farms and reduced efficacy of macrocyclic lactones, a class of deworming medicines, in some investigations. The outcomes were egg-count reductions, not direct proof of how many horses were clinically ill. Regional reports cannot establish the resistance status of a particular barn without testing. Before interpreting a poor reduction, the veterinary team reviews the product, administration, horse weights, specimens and laboratory method. The result can then guide a revised programme rather than encourage unplanned repeat dosing by the owner.

A separate Swedish study found mean ivermectin egg-count reductions exceeding 99 percent in all sixteen participating establishments. Egg reappearance periods ranged from six to more than eight weeks. Egg reappearance period means how soon shedding resumes after initial suppression; it is different from the early reduction test. Young horses in that study tended to shed again sooner. This provides an instructive contrast with farms showing poor efficacy: drug performance cannot be assumed to be identical everywhere. The selected establishments largely practiced selective treatment, but the observational design cannot prove that this practice alone caused retained efficacy. Preserve both the successful measurement and that limit.

Another Swedish field study documented reduced pyrantel efficacy and found no corresponding change in the broad cyathostomin species composition examined. Identifying which species are present therefore did not, by itself, explain whether the medicine worked. A parasite population can retain a similar species mixture while resistant worms survive within it. FECRT measures the population's response through egg shedding, rather than giving the horse a permanent personal label of resistance. A new horse can also introduce a different parasite population to a property. Treatment records, arrival history and appropriately repeated efficacy checks make this biological distinction useful in a practical farm programme.

sections.heading: Real outbreaks with low or absent egg counts

paragraphs.text: Lawson and colleagues reviewed 38 horses admitted to two hospitals with larval cyathostominosis, a disease caused by small strongyle larvae developing in and emerging from the intestinal wall. Twenty-one were nonsurvivors, including three dead on arrival. Among the 21 horses with a fecal egg count, the median was only 50 EPG. This was a selected hospital population, not the risk for a healthy horse with a low count. It nevertheless demonstrates how serious disease from larval stages can coexist with little egg shedding. Blood protein measurements, inflammatory findings, ultrasound, clinical course and fecal or postmortem evidence contributed to investigation. Associations between treatment and nonsurvival in this retrospective series should not be read as proof that supportive treatment caused death; the sickest animals may require the most intervention.

An Irish outbreak affecting a herd of 23 horses provides another outcome record. Fourteen developed overt signs consistent with acute larval cyathostominosis; two were euthanized and twelve recovered. Postmortem tissue from the fatal cases showed severe intestinal inflammation and damage associated with cyathostomin larvae. The investigators also studied altered fecal bacterial communities, but the small descriptive series could not isolate a single cause of each animal's susceptibility. The recoveries show that the syndrome was not uniformly fatal, while the deaths show why a clinical deterioration requires attention. No single egg-count threshold in that study could be adopted as a universal predictor of who would live or die.

A 2025 report described nine young Thoroughbreds with suspected acute larval cyathostominosis on one Irish stud farm. All nine samples were reported as zero EPG, yet fourth-stage larvae were found in six horses. One horse was euthanized and eight recovered. The report describes a well-managed establishment, but also records absent parasite diagnostics and farm treatment records, with no dung removal or mixed grazing. Those reported gaps qualify the description of the farm. Zero detectable eggs did not exclude larval disease. Even larval examination was negative in some suspected cases, so its absence also did not settle every diagnosis.

sections.heading: Fatal disease does not create a simple neglect test

paragraphs.text: An Ontario review identified 24 equids with larval cyathostominosis at postmortem between 1991 and 2003. The investigators judged it the primary cause of clinical illness in nineteen, while five had other major diseases despite compatible intestinal signs. Some animals lacked striking gross lesions, and microscopic examination documented the larvae and associated inflammation. This is a useful forensic distinction: finding parasites, attributing the animal's illness and identifying its cause of death are separate judgments. The selected necropsy records could not provide a survival rate among all exposed horses. They also cannot establish neglect merely because larvae were found. Husbandry, treatment access, clinical timeline and competing disease require their own evidence.

Parascaris roundworms can obstruct the small intestine in young horses, a problem that an adult strongyle monitoring category does not describe. Tatz and colleagues reported fifteen horses undergoing surgery for ascarid impaction: twelve survived to discharge and nine survived at least a year. The authors described associations between surgical approach and outcome, but the retrospective series was small and could not separate every treatment effect from disease severity or other changes in care. These were horses with surgically confirmed obstruction, not horses selected by a particular EPG cutoff. A painful, distended or deteriorating foal needs veterinary assessment regardless of whether a previous fecal report looked reassuring.

A later Scandinavian surgical review found fourteen Parascaris impactions among the juvenile horses investigated. Four survived to discharge. Of the three discharged foals with long-term information, one was euthanized about a year later for an uncertain reason, and two were known to survive for years; the fourth outcome was unknown. Several had received anthelmintics shortly before colic, while three had never been treated. Timing alone did not establish that treatment caused the obstruction. The markedly different outcome from the fifteen-horse series also warns against presenting one hospital's survival percentage as a universal prognosis. Preserve the case selection, confirmation method and missing follow-up when using such reports to explain risk.
